◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

dbt is the most important tool in modern analytics engineering. Every modern data team uses it or wants to. Every job description for analytics engineer, analyst, or data engineer lists dbt. Understanding what dbt is and why it exists is the foundation for everything else in the modern data stack.

What dbt is

dbt (data build tool) is the T in ELT — the transformation layer that runs inside your data warehouse. You write SQL files; dbt compiles them, runs them in dependency order, and produces tables and views in your warehouse.

DBT IN ONE SENTENCE
dbt lets you transform data inside your warehouse using SQL + Jinja,
with version control, testing, and documentation built in.

The ELT vs ETL shift

The fundamental shift dbt rides on:

ETL (old) Extract → Transform (external server) → Load to warehouse
ELT (new) Extract → Load to warehouse → Transform (in warehouse, via dbt)

Why ELT won:

  • Cloud warehouses got powerful — Snowflake/BigQuery scale instantly
  • Storage is cheap — load everything raw, transform later
  • SQL is the lingua franca — analysts already know it
  • Iteration is fast — change a SQL file, rerun, see results

The modern data stack

Sources (Postgres, Salesforce, Stripe, GA4, ...)
     ↓
Extract + Load tool (Fivetran, Airbyte, Meltano)
     ↓
Cloud warehouse (Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks / Redshift)
     ↓
dbt (transforms raw data into clean models)  ← YOU ARE HERE
     ↓
BI tools (Looker, Tableau, Mode, Hex, Power BI)
     ↓
Business users + analysts

What dbt actually does

Three core capabilities:

  1. Compile + run SQL — your .sql files become tables/views in dependency order
  2. Test data — declarative tests on columns and relationships
  3. Generate documentation — searchable docs site with lineage graph

Analytics engineering

dbt created (or solidified) a new job title: analytics engineer. The role sits between data engineers (pipelines) and analysts (BI):

Data engineer Pipelines, infrastructure, getting data into the warehouse
Analytics engineer Models the data — turns raw into clean — with dbt
Analyst / Data scientist Asks questions using the modeled data

dbt Core vs dbt Cloud

# dbt Core
# - Open source, free, MIT licensed
# - CLI tool: dbt run, dbt test, dbt docs
# - You run it: locally, on a server, in Airflow, in GitHub Actions
# - Pip install: pip install dbt-snowflake (or other adapter)

# dbt Cloud
# - SaaS offering by dbt Labs (the company)
# - Adds: web IDE, job scheduling, CI/CD, hosted docs, semantic layer
# - Built on top of dbt Core
# - Free tier for 1 developer; paid for teams
★ WHICH TO USE

For learning: dbt Core locally. For small teams: dbt Cloud's free developer tier. For larger teams: dbt Cloud (teams plan) or dbt Core with your own orchestrator (Airflow/Prefect/Dagster).

Why every data team adopts dbt

The pre-dbt world looked like this:

  • SQL scripts scattered across team members' laptops
  • No version control for transformations
  • "Don't run that until I tell you" coordination
  • Same metric computed differently in 5 places
  • Documentation lives in Confluence (out of date)
  • Testing? What testing?

dbt fixes all of this by bringing software-engineering practices to analytics: Git, modular code, testing, docs, CI/CD.

Walk through it: a project of eight models runs with dbt run. dbt reads the ref() calls, orders the models into a graph, runs the three staging views first, then the tables and the incremental model that depend on them, then the report that depends on those, four at a time. Each line names what was built and where; the summary says all seven succeeded. That is what dbt is: SQL files in, a dependency-ordered build in the warehouse out.

▸ A SIMPLE DBT MODEL
# models/marts/fct_orders.sql
-- This file becomes a table called fct_orders in your warehouse

{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    order_date,
    amount_usd
from {{ ref('stg_app__orders') }}    -- references another dbt model
where status = 'completed'

# That's it. dbt:
# 1. Compiles {{ ref() }} into the actual table name
# 2. Determines this depends on stg_app__orders
# 3. Runs stg_app__orders first, then this one
# 4. Creates the table in your warehouse
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • dbt = data build tool; the T in ELT; transforms data inside the warehouse
  • SQL + Jinja templates compiled and run in dependency order
  • Modern data stack: extract → warehouse → dbt → BI tools
  • dbt Core (open-source CLI) vs dbt Cloud (SaaS with IDE + scheduling)
  • Created the analytics engineering role between data eng and analyst
  • Brings software-engineering practices (Git, tests, docs) to analytics
  • Adopted at most modern data teams; required skill for analytics engineering jobs

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Setting up dbt right the first time saves hours of confusion. The install + profile + first dbt debug success is the foundation; once it works, you can iterate fast. Most "dbt isn't working" issues at companies are bad profiles or adapter version mismatches.

Installation

dbt is a Python package. You install the adapter for your warehouse, which brings in dbt-core:

# Create a Python virtual environment (recommended)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS/Linux
# .venvScriptsactivate     # Windows

# Install the adapter for your warehouse:
pip install dbt-snowflake     # Snowflake
pip install dbt-bigquery      # BigQuery
pip install dbt-databricks    # Databricks
pip install dbt-redshift      # Redshift
pip install dbt-postgres      # Postgres

# Verify install
dbt --version

The two key files

dbt_project.yml Lives at repo root. Defines the project: name, version, paths, materialization defaults.
profiles.yml Lives in ~/.dbt/ (outside the repo!). Contains warehouse credentials per target environment.
⚠ NEVER COMMIT profiles.yml

It contains passwords/keys. Keep it in ~/.dbt/profiles.yml (your home folder), outside the project repo entirely. If you must include a sample, name it profiles.example.yml with placeholders.

A profiles.yml for Snowflake

# ~/.dbt/profiles.yml

my_project:                          # matches "profile:" in dbt_project.yml
  target: dev                        # default target when you run dbt
  outputs:
    dev:                             # individual dev profile
      type: snowflake
      account: abc12345.us-east-1
      user: natasha
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: ANALYTICS_DEV
      warehouse: DEV_WH
      database: DEV
      schema: dbt_natasha            # YOUR sandbox schema
      threads: 4
      keepalives_idle: 240
    
    prod:                            # production profile
      type: snowflake
      account: abc12345.us-east-1
      user: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PROD_USER') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PROD_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: ANALYTICS_PROD
      warehouse: PROD_WH
      database: ANALYTICS
      schema: analytics              # canonical prod schema
      threads: 8

Using environment variables for secrets

# In profiles.yml, reference env vars:
password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') }}"

# Set them in your shell:
export SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD='your_password_here'

# Or use a .env file + direnv / dotenv
# .env
SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD=your_password_here

# Never put plaintext passwords in profiles.yml!

dbt debug — the first command to run

# From inside your dbt project directory:
dbt debug

# Output you want to see:
# dbt version: 1.7.0
# Connection test: [OK connection ok]
# All checks passed!

# If it fails, you'll see exactly where:
# - Wrong account format? Says so.
# - Bad credentials? Says so.
# - Schema doesn't exist? Says so.

# Fix one issue at a time, rerun dbt debug until clean.

Common debug failures

Error Fix
Authentication failed Wrong password / user / role — check spelling, MFA settings
Database does not exist Verify database name; create if needed; check role has access
Schema does not exist dbt usually auto-creates it; manually create if perms missing
SSL / network errors Check VPN, firewall, account URL format
No profile named X Check name matches between profiles.yml and dbt_project.yml

dbt init — creating a new project

# Initialize a new dbt project
dbt init my_project

# Walks you through:
# - Database adapter selection
# - Connection parameters
# - Generates profiles.yml entry in ~/.dbt/
# - Creates project folder with starter structure

# After init, you have:
my_project/
├── dbt_project.yml
├── models/
│   └── example/
├── seeds/
├── tests/
├── analyses/
├── macros/
├── snapshots/
└── README.md

# Verify with:
cd my_project
dbt debug
dbt run --select example   # builds the example models

VS Code setup

Recommended VS Code extensions for dbt:

  • dbt Power User — autocomplete, lineage, query previews
  • vscode-dbt — syntax highlighting for dbt SQL
  • Jinja — Jinja syntax
  • YAML — YAML schema validation
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — profiles.yml and dbt debug
crteam:
  target: dev
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: duckdb
      path: warehouse.duckdb
      schema: dev_natasha
      threads: 4
    prod:
      type: duckdb
      path: warehouse.duckdb
      schema: analytics
      threads: 4

Walk through it: the profile has one entry per environment: dev writes to a personal schema, prod to analytics, both on the same warehouse. dbt debug is the first command to run after any setup: it finds both files, loads the adapter, and makes a real connection. When it prints "All checks passed", every later problem is in your SQL, not your setup.

▸ FROM ZERO TO FIRST RUN
# Full setup, ~10 minutes:

# 1. Install
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install dbt-snowflake

# 2. Init project
dbt init my_analytics
# Answer the prompts (account, user, role, warehouse, db, schema)

# 3. Move to project
cd my_analytics

# 4. Verify
dbt debug
# All checks passed!

# 5. Run the example models
dbt run --select example
# Creates my_first_dbt_model and my_second_dbt_model tables

# 6. Test them
dbt test --select example
# All tests pass

# 7. Generate docs
dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve
# Opens browser; you can navigate the lineage
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Install via pip: pip install dbt-<adapter>
  • Use a Python venv to isolate dbt's deps
  • Two key files: dbt_project.yml (in repo) and profiles.yml (in ~/.dbt/)
  • Never commit profiles.yml — credentials live in env vars
  • Run dbt debug first to verify the setup
  • dbt init scaffolds a new project
  • VS Code + dbt Power User extension is the most common dev setup

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every dbt project follows the same folder structure. Knowing what goes where lets you read any dbt repo on GitHub or your team's codebase instantly. Following the convention also makes dbt's tooling (lineage, tests, docs) work correctly out of the box.

Standard dbt project layout

my_dbt_project/
├── dbt_project.yml          ← project config (REQUIRED)
├── packages.yml             ← package dependencies
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
│
├── models/                  ← THE main folder; SQL transformations
│   ├── staging/             ← stg_ models (1:1 with sources)
│   ├── intermediate/        ← int_ models (joins, logic)
│   └── marts/               ← fct_/dim_ models (consumable)
│
├── seeds/                   ← CSV files loaded as tables
├── snapshots/               ← SCD2 history tracking
├── macros/                  ← reusable SQL/Jinja functions
├── tests/                   ← custom singular tests
├── analyses/                ← one-off queries (not built as models)
│
├── target/                  ← compiled SQL (gitignored)
├── dbt_packages/            ← installed packages (gitignored)
└── logs/                    ← run logs (gitignored)

dbt_project.yml — the master config

# dbt_project.yml
name: 'my_analytics'
version: '1.0.0'
config-version: 2
profile: 'my_analytics'        ← matches profiles.yml key

# Path configurations (defaults are fine usually)
model-paths: ["models"]
seed-paths: ["seeds"]
test-paths: ["tests"]
analysis-paths: ["analyses"]
macro-paths: ["macros"]
snapshot-paths: ["snapshots"]
target-path: "target"          ← compiled SQL output
clean-targets:
  - "target"
  - "dbt_packages"

# Materialization defaults per folder
models:
  my_analytics:                ← matches "name" above
    staging:
      +materialized: view      ← all stg_ models default to view
      +schema: staging         ← schema suffix
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral ← int_ compiled into downstream
      +schema: intermediate
    marts:
      +materialized: table     ← marts default to table
      +schema: marts

# Variables (referenced via {{ var('name') }})
vars:
  start_date: '2020-01-01'
  exclude_test_customers: true

models/ — where everything lives

Models are .sql files. Each becomes a table or view in your warehouse. dbt determines build order automatically from ref() calls.

models/
├── staging/
│   ├── stripe/
│   │   ├── _stripe__sources.yml   ← source declarations
│   │   ├── _stripe__models.yml    ← model docs + tests
│   │   ├── stg_stripe__charges.sql
│   │   ├── stg_stripe__customers.sql
│   │   └── stg_stripe__refunds.sql
│   └── app/
│       ├── _app__sources.yml
│       ├── _app__models.yml
│       ├── stg_app__orders.sql
│       ├── stg_app__users.sql
│       └── stg_app__products.sql
│
├── intermediate/
│   ├── finance/
│   │   ├── _finance__models.yml
│   │   └── int_orders_with_refunds.sql
│   └── customer/
│       └── int_customers_enriched.sql
│
└── marts/
    ├── finance/
    │   ├── _finance__models.yml
    │   ├── fct_orders.sql
    │   └── fct_subscription_periods.sql
    └── core/
        ├── dim_customers.sql
        ├── dim_products.sql
        └── dim_date.sql
★ NAMING CONVENTIONS
  • stg_<source>__<entity> — staging models (double underscore!)
  • int_<area>_<purpose> — intermediate
  • fct_<event> — fact tables
  • dim_<entity> — dimensions

YAML files start with underscore (e.g., _stripe__sources.yml) so they sort to the top of file listings.

seeds/ — CSV files as tables

For small static reference data: country codes, holidays, mapping tables.

# seeds/country_codes.csv
country_code,country_name,region
US,United States,North America
UK,United Kingdom,Europe
DE,Germany,Europe

# Run: dbt seed
# Creates a table called "country_codes" in your warehouse

# Reference in a model:
select * from {{ ref('country_codes') }}

snapshots/ — SCD2 history

Special dbt feature for tracking slowly changing dimensions.

# snapshots/customers_snapshot.sql
{% snapshot customers_snapshot %}
{{
    config(
      target_schema='snapshots',
      unique_key='customer_id',
      strategy='check',
      check_cols=['name', 'email', 'segment']
    )
}}
select * from {{ source('app', 'customers') }}
{% endsnapshot %}

# Run: dbt snapshot
# Auto-tracks changes over time

macros/ — reusable code

# macros/cents_to_dollars.sql
{% macro cents_to_dollars(column_name, precision=2) %}
    round({{ column_name }} / 100.0, {{ precision }})
{% endmacro %}

# Use in models:
select
    order_id,
    {{ cents_to_dollars('amount_cents') }} as amount_usd
from {{ ref('stg_stripe__charges') }}

tests/ — custom test queries

# tests/assert_revenue_consistency.sql
-- Test: monthly revenue from fct_orders matches what's in fct_metrics_monthly
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount_usd) AS rev_from_orders
    FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
    GROUP BY 1
) o
JOIN {{ ref('fct_metrics_monthly') }} m USING (month)
WHERE ABS(o.rev_from_orders - m.revenue) > 0.01

# Test FAILS if any rows return.
# Test PASSES if zero rows return.

analyses/ — exploratory queries

SQL files that get compiled but NOT built as models. Use for ad-hoc analysis you want versioned.

What gets gitignored

# .gitignore for any dbt project
target/              # compiled SQL (rebuilt each run)
dbt_packages/        # installed packages (run dbt deps)
logs/                # run logs
.user.yml            # user-specific settings
profiles.yml         # NEVER commit
*.pyc
__pycache__/
.env
.DS_Store
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the files of a small, complete project
$ find . -path ./target -prune -o -path ./logs -prune -o -type f -print | grep -v duckdb | sort ./.gitignore ./dbt_project.yml ./macros/cents_to_dollars.sql ./macros/safe_divide.sql ./models/exposures.yml ./models/intermediate/int_orders__joined.sql ./models/marts/_marts__models.yml ./models/marts/dim_customers.sql ./models/marts/fct_events.sql ./models/marts/fct_orders.sql ./models/marts/rpt_product_pivot.sql ./models/staging/app/_app__sources.yml ./models/staging/app/stg_app__customers.sql ./models/staging/app/stg_app__events.sql ./models/staging/app/stg_app__orders.sql ./profiles.yml ./snapshots/customers_snapshot.sql ./tests/assert_revenue_positive.sql ./tests/generic/assert_positive_value.sql
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: this is the project every dbt lesson in this course runs against. dbt_project.yml names the project and sets per-folder defaults; models/ holds staging, intermediate and marts with their YAML beside them; macros/, tests/ and snapshots/ each hold one kind of thing. .gitignore keeps target/, logs and the local database out of the repository. Any dbt repo on GitHub reads the same way.

▸ READING A REAL DBT PROJECT
# Encountering a new dbt repo for the first time

# 1. Read dbt_project.yml first
# - What's the project name? Default materializations?
# - What variables are defined? Common configs?

# 2. Browse models/staging/ to see what sources exist
# - One subfolder per source = list of data systems
# - .yml files declare the actual source schema

# 3. Browse models/marts/ to see the consumable output
# - These are what BI tools query
# - fct_/dim_ prefixes tell you the table type

# 4. Browse models/intermediate/ to see business logic
# - This is where complex transforms live
# - int_ models bridge staging and marts

# 5. Check packages.yml
# - dbt_utils almost always present
# - codegen, dbt_date, dbt_expectations are common

# 6. Run dbt docs generate + dbt docs serve
# - Visual lineage graph
# - Searchable docs
# - The fastest way to understand the project
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Standard layout: models/, seeds/, snapshots/, macros/, tests/, analyses/
  • dbt_project.yml is the master config (paths, materializations, vars)
  • Models split by layer: staging/, intermediate/, marts/
  • Sub-folders within layers organize by source or business area
  • YAML files start with underscore for sort order
  • Seeds = static CSV data; Snapshots = SCD2; Macros = reusable code
  • Always gitignore: target/, dbt_packages/, logs/, profiles.yml, .env
  • To understand a new repo: read dbt_project.yml, browse staging then marts, run dbt docs

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Writing your first dbt model is the moment dbt clicks. You write SQL, run a command, and a table appears in your warehouse with full lineage tracking. After this, everything else in dbt is variations on the same theme.

The simplest possible dbt model

# models/my_first_model.sql
select 1 as id, 'hello' as message

# Run it:
dbt run --select my_first_model

# Result: a table called "my_first_model" appears in your warehouse
# in the schema specified by your profiles.yml dev target

# Inspect:
# SELECT * FROM my_dev_schema.my_first_model;
#  id | message
#   1 | hello

That's it. The file becomes a table. The file's name becomes the table's name.

A more realistic model

# models/staging/stg_app__orders.sql

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('app', 'orders') }}
),

renamed as (
    select
        id              as order_id,
        customer_id,
        amount_cents / 100.0 as amount_usd,
        status,
        created_at::timestamp as created_at,
        case when status = 'completed' then true else false end as is_completed
    from source
    where created_at >= '2020-01-01'   -- skip ancient test data
)

select * from renamed

Things to notice:

  • {{ source('app', 'orders') }} — Jinja reference to a declared source
  • CTEs (with ... as) organize logic readably
  • Pattern: source → renamed → final SELECT
  • Light cleanup only — staging shouldn't have heavy logic

Declaring sources

Before referencing a source with {{ source() }}, declare it in YAML:

# models/staging/app/_app__sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: app                    ← used in {{ source('app', ...) }}
    description: Our SaaS application's Postgres replica
    database: raw                ← warehouse database
    schema: app_replica          ← warehouse schema
    tables:
      - name: orders
        description: One row per order placed
        columns:
          - name: id
            description: Primary key
            tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customers
        description: One row per customer
      - name: products

Referencing other models

# models/marts/fct_orders.sql

{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,        -- from dim_customers
    o.order_date,
    o.amount_usd
from {{ ref('stg_app__orders') }} o
left join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c using (customer_id)
where o.is_completed = true

{{ ref('stg_app__orders') }} compiles to the actual table name. This is how dbt builds the DAG.

Running models

# Run all models
dbt run

# Run a specific model
dbt run --select fct_orders

# Run a model AND all its downstream dependencies
dbt run --select fct_orders+

# Run a model AND all its upstream dependencies
dbt run --select +fct_orders

# Run everything in a folder
dbt run --select staging

# Run multiple models
dbt run --select fct_orders dim_customers

# Run with full refresh (for incrementals)
dbt run --full-refresh

What happens when you run

  1. dbt parses all .sql files in models/
  2. Builds a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) from ref() calls
  3. Compiles Jinja → pure SQL (saved in target/compiled/)
  4. Wraps each in a CREATE TABLE / CREATE VIEW statement
  5. Runs them in dependency order (parallel where possible)
  6. Reports successes and failures

Inspecting compiled SQL

# See exactly what SQL dbt is running
cat target/compiled/my_project/models/marts/fct_orders.sql

# Or:
dbt compile --select fct_orders
# Compiles without running; outputs to target/compiled/

# The compiled SQL has all ref() and source() resolved to actual table names
# This is what your warehouse actually executes

Materializations

view (default) Creates a view; recomputed on every query. Fast to build; slow to query.
table Creates a real table; data stored. Slow to build; fast to query.
incremental Only inserts new rows. Best for big append-only tables (events).
ephemeral Not materialized; compiled into downstream model as CTE. 
# Set materialization in the model:
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select * from {{ ref('staging_model') }}

# Or set in dbt_project.yml (applies to a whole folder):
models:
  my_project:
    marts:
      +materialized: table
    staging:
      +materialized: view

Compiling vs running

# dbt compile  — generates compiled SQL files, does NOT execute
# dbt run      — compiles AND executes against the warehouse
# dbt build    — compiles, runs, tests (all in one)
# dbt test     — runs only tests
# dbt docs     — generates / serves documentation

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('app', 'orders') }}
),
renamed as (
    select
        id            as order_id,
        customer_id,
        product,
        amount_cents,
        status,
        ordered_at
    from source
)
select * from renamed

[RUN] 1 of 1 OK created sql view model dev_natasha.stg_app__orders ................... [OK in 0.08s] Finished running 1 view model in 0 hours 0 minutes and 0.23 seconds (0.23s). Completed successfully Done. The compiled file in target/compiled shows what dbt actually sent: the Jinja call became the fully qualified "warehouse"."raw"."orders", and everything else is the SQL you wrote. When something looks wrong, this compiled file is where you look first.

from {{ ref('stg_app__orders') }}

  • File name = table name; folder structure = organization

  • {{ ref('model_name') }} = reference another dbt model (builds DAG)
  • Sources declared in YAML files first; then referenced in SQL
  • CTE-based style (with ... as) is the convention
  • Materializations: view (default), table, incremental, ephemeral

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The ref() function is the single most important feature in dbt. It's what builds the DAG, enables lineage tracking, and makes your project deployable across environments without changing a single line of SQL. Understanding ref() deeply unlocks everything else.

What ref() does

{{ ref('model_name') }} is a Jinja function that compiles to the fully-qualified table name of another dbt model:

# In your model SQL:
select * from {{ ref('stg_app__orders') }}

# Compiled in DEV environment:
select * from dev_db.dev_natasha.stg_app__orders

# Compiled in PROD environment:
select * from analytics.analytics.stg_app__orders

# Same SQL file. Different output. Magic.

Why not hardcode table names?

# BAD — hardcoded
select * from analytics.dim_customers
# Problems:
# - Wrong in dev (no access to prod schema)
# - Breaks if you rename the schema
# - Breaks if a teammate has a different sandbox
# - No lineage tracking

# GOOD — ref()
select * from {{ ref('dim_customers') }}
# Wins:
# - Auto-resolves to current target's schema
# - Lineage shows fct_orders depends on dim_customers
# - dbt builds dim_customers BEFORE fct_orders automatically
# - Refactor-safe (rename a model, all refs update)

The DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)

dbt builds a graph from every ref() call. The graph determines run order.

# Project structure with refs:

# stg_app__orders.sql       ← from source
# stg_app__customers.sql    ← from source
# stg_stripe__charges.sql   ← from source

# int_orders_with_charges.sql
#   uses ref('stg_app__orders'), ref('stg_stripe__charges')

# dim_customers.sql
#   uses ref('stg_app__customers')

# fct_orders.sql
#   uses ref('int_orders_with_charges'), ref('dim_customers')

# DAG that dbt builds:
#
#   stg_app__orders ────┐
#                       ├──> int_orders_with_charges ──┐
#   stg_stripe__charges─┘                              ├──> fct_orders
#                                                      │
#   stg_app__customers ───> dim_customers ─────────────┘

# When you run dbt run, dbt:
# 1. Builds all stg_ models in parallel (no deps between them)
# 2. Then int_orders_with_charges + dim_customers in parallel
# 3. Then fct_orders

The source() function

For raw source data (not built by dbt), use source():

# Reference declared source
select * from {{ source('app', 'orders') }}

# Compiles to:
select * from raw.app_replica.orders

# Sources are declared in YAML first:
sources:
  - name: app
    database: raw
    schema: app_replica
    tables:
      - name: orders

Why source() instead of ref()?

Sources are the BOUNDARY between your dbt project and the outside world. Tracking them as sources gives you:

  • Lineage from external data → through dbt → to final marts
  • Freshness checks (dbt source freshness)
  • Easy source tracing — search "where is this data from" in dbt docs
  • Schema isolation — change source schema/db without touching SQL

Cross-project refs (dbt 1.5+)

Reference models from another dbt project (advanced; team-of-teams setup):

# In dbt_project.yml of consumer:
projects:
  - name: shared_marts

# Reference:
select * from {{ ref('shared_marts', 'dim_customers') }}

# Useful when:
# - Different teams own different dbt projects
# - You want to share dims/facts across teams
# - Avoiding monorepo

The {{ this }} reference

Inside a model, {{ this }} resolves to the current model's fully-qualified name. Useful for incremental models:

# In an incremental fct_events.sql:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='event_id') }}

select *
from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts > (select max(event_ts) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# {{ this }} = the table being built right now
# Lets you query the existing version during incremental builds

Selecting models on the DAG

dbt's --select flag uses graph operators to pick models:

dbt run --select fct_orders Just fct_orders
dbt run --select +fct_orders fct_orders + all upstream
dbt run --select fct_orders+ fct_orders + all downstream
dbt run --select +fct_orders+ Full lineage (up + down)
dbt run --select staging Everything in staging/ folder
dbt run --select tag:finance Models tagged 'finance'
dbt run --select state:modified Only models changed vs prior state
dbt run --exclude tag:slow Everything EXCEPT models tagged slow

Common ref() pitfalls

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES
  • Cyclical dependencies — ref() loop. dbt errors out. Restructure to break the cycle.
  • Hardcoded table names slipped in — code review catches; dbt itself can't detect.
  • Disabled models still in refs — fails compilation. Either enable or remove the ref.
  • Typo in model name — error: "Compilation Error: ref('X') not found"

Lineage visualization

# Generate docs with lineage graph
dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve

# Opens browser at localhost:8080
# - Click any model
# - See "Lineage" tab
# - Visual graph of refs upstream + downstream
# - Best way to understand a project
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what ref() compiles to, and the graph it builds
select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    product,
    {{ cents_to_dollars('amount_cents') }} as amount_usd,
    status,
    segment,
    ordered_at
from {{ ref('int_orders__joined') }}
where ordered_at >= '{{ var("start_date") }}'
{% if target.name == 'prod' %}
  and status != 'test'
{% endif %}
$ cat target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/fct_orders.sql with __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined as ( select o.*, c.segment, c.country from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__orders" o left join "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__customers" c using (customer_id) ) select order_id, customer_id, product, round(amount_cents / 100.0, 2) as amount_usd, status, segment, ordered_at from __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined where ordered_at >= '2026-01-01' $ dbt ls --select +fct_orders --resource-type model crteam.marts.fct_orders crteam.intermediate.int_orders__joined crteam.staging.app.stg_app__customers crteam.staging.app.stg_app__orders
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: the model references an intermediate model and calls a macro. Compiled, the ref() became the intermediate model's SQL inlined as a CTE (it is ephemeral), the staging refs inside it became fully qualified names in the dev_natasha schema, and the macro became round(amount_cents / 100.0, 2). Change the target to prod and the same file compiles against analytics without an edit. dbt ls --select +fct_orders walks the graph upstream: the model, its intermediate, and the two staging models it depends on.

▸ TRACING A REAL PROJECT'S LINEAGE
# You inherit a project. Where does fct_marketing_attribution come from?

# Open dbt docs → search "fct_marketing_attribution" → lineage tab
# 
# You see:
#
#  source(salesforce.opportunities) ─┐
#                                    ├─> stg_salesforce__opportunities ─┐
#  source(salesforce.accounts) ──────┘                                  │
#                                                                       ├─> int_opportunities_with_touches ─┐
#  source(marketing.touches) ──> stg_marketing__touches ────────────────┘                                   │
#                                                                                                           ├─> fct_marketing_attribution
#  source(app.users) ──> stg_app__users ──> dim_users ────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
#
# Now you understand the full chain.
# No documentation needed — the lineage IS the documentation.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • {{ ref('model') }} = reference another dbt model; builds DAG
  • {{ source('schema', 'table') }} = reference raw source (declared in YAML)
  • Refs make SQL environment-agnostic (dev/staging/prod all work)
  • dbt builds models in dependency order automatically (parallel where possible)
  • Selector syntax: + for upstream, + for downstream, both for full lineage
  • {{ this }} = current model name; useful in incrementals
  • Cross-project refs: ref('project', 'model')
  • Lineage graph in dbt docs is the best way to understand any project

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Materializations are the single biggest performance lever in dbt. Pick the wrong one and your dbt run takes hours; pick the right one and it takes minutes. Understanding view/table/incremental/ephemeral lets you make informed trade-offs between build time, query speed, and freshness.

The four materialization types

MATERIALIZATIONS
view: CREATE VIEW; logical, recomputed on query
table: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT; physical, stored
incremental: INSERT/MERGE new rows only
ephemeral: inlined as CTE; not materialized

view materialization

# models/staging/stg_orders.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

select
    id as order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount_usd
from {{ source('app', 'orders') }}

# What dbt creates in warehouse:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW dev_schema.stg_orders AS
    select id as order_id, customer_id, amount_usd 
    from raw.app.orders;

# Pros:
# - Fast to build (just creates a view, no data move)
# - Always fresh (reflects underlying source)
# - Cheap on storage

# Cons:
# - Slow to query (recomputes every time)
# - Compounds across layers (view on view on view)
# - Some warehouses limit nesting depth

Use view for: staging models, simple transformations, small datasets.

table materialization

# models/marts/fct_orders.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select * from {{ ref('int_orders_enriched') }}

# What dbt creates:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE analytics.fct_orders AS
    select * from analytics.int_orders_enriched;

# Pros:
# - Fast queries (data is materialized)
# - Predictable performance
# - Decouples query speed from source complexity

# Cons:
# - Slow to build (full rewrite each dbt run)
# - More storage (every dbt run = full table)
# - Stale until next rebuild

Use table for: mart-layer fact and dimension tables, anything queried often.

incremental materialization

The performance winner for large append-only tables. Instead of rebuilding the whole table, INSERT only new rows.

# models/marts/fct_events.sql
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns'
) }}

select
    event_id,
    user_id,
    event_type,
    event_ts,
    properties
from {{ ref('stg_events') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- Only process new events since last run
  where event_ts > (select max(event_ts) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# First run: full table build
# Subsequent runs: only inserts where event_ts > existing max

The is_incremental() macro

Returns TRUE only on incremental runs (table exists and you're not doing --full-refresh):

# Common pattern: filter only on incremental runs
select * from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts > (select max(event_ts) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# is_incremental() is TRUE when:
# 1. The model is materialized='incremental'
# 2. The target table already exists
# 3. You did NOT pass --full-refresh

# Otherwise FALSE (does a full build)

Incremental strategies

append Just INSERT. Fast. Doesn't handle late-arriving updates.
merge (default) MERGE: update matching unique_keys, insert new. Handles updates.
delete+insert DELETE matching keys, then INSERT. Postgres-friendly.
insert_overwrite Replace partitions. Best for partitioned BigQuery / Spark tables. 
# Specifying strategy
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge'   -- explicit
) }}

Handling schema changes

# What happens when you add a new column to an incremental model?

{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns'  -- recommended
) }}

# Options for on_schema_change:
# - 'ignore' (default): old columns kept; new columns NOT added
# - 'append_new_columns': new columns added; old kept
# - 'sync_all_columns': new added, removed dropped (destructive)
# - 'fail': error if schema changes

# Most teams use 'append_new_columns' for safety

ephemeral materialization

Not materialized at all. dbt inlines the SQL as a CTE in downstream models.

# models/intermediate/int_orders_filtered.sql
{{ config(materialized='ephemeral') }}

select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} 
where status = 'completed'

# Downstream model:
select * from {{ ref('int_orders_filtered') }}

# Compiles to:
WITH __dbt__cte__int_orders_filtered AS (
    select * from analytics.stg_orders where status = 'completed'
)
select * from __dbt__cte__int_orders_filtered

# Pros: no storage, always fresh
# Cons: can't query directly; compiles into every downstream model

Use ephemeral for: simple intermediate transforms that are used by only one or two downstream models.

Choosing materialization

Staging (small, light cleaning) view
Intermediate (joins/logic, used 1-2 places) ephemeral
Intermediate (used many places) view or table
Marts (consumable, queried often) table
Large append-only facts (events, logs) incremental
Slowly-changing dimensions table + snapshots (separate)

Setting defaults in dbt_project.yml

# dbt_project.yml
models:
  my_project:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral
    marts:
      +materialized: table
      events:
        +materialized: incremental   # override for events subfolder

# Override per-model in the model file:
# {{ config(materialized='view') }}
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the DDL each materialization produces
models:
  crteam:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral
    marts:
      +materialized: table
$ echo '-- target/run/.../stg_app__customers.sql'; cat target/run/crteam/models/staging/app/stg_app__customers.sql; echo; echo '-- target/run/.../dim_customers.sql'; cat target/run/crteam/models/marts/dim_customers.sql -- target/run/.../stg_app__customers.sql create view "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__customers__dbt_tmp" as ( select id as customer_id, email, segment, country from "warehouse"."raw"."customers" ); -- target/run/.../dim_customers.sql create table "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."dim_customers__dbt_tmp" as ( select customer_id, email, segment, country from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__customers" );
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: the project file sets a default per folder. The files in target/run are the statements dbt executed: the staging model became CREATE VIEW, the mart became CREATE TABLE ... AS. The intermediate model produced no statement at all: it is ephemeral, so it appears only as the CTE inside fct_orders (previous section). Same SQL in the model file, three very different objects in the warehouse.

▸ INCREMENTAL ORDERS — REAL PATTERN
# Original full-refresh model (rebuilds 100M rows daily = 30 min)
{{ config(materialized='table') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# After making incremental (rebuilds ~50k new rows = 30 sec)
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='order_id',
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns'
) }}

select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount_usd,
    order_ts,
    status
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- Include slight overlap to catch late-arriving data
  where order_ts >= (select max(order_ts) - interval '3 days' from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# Backfill / refresh:
# dbt run --select fct_orders --full-refresh
# (Bypasses incremental, rebuilds from scratch)
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • view: cheap to build, slow to query; default for staging
  • table: slow to build, fast to query; default for marts
  • incremental: INSERT only new rows; for large append-only tables
  • ephemeral: not materialized; inlined as CTE downstream
  • is_incremental() filters source to new rows on incremental runs
  • Incremental strategies: append, merge (default), delete+insert, insert_overwrite
  • on_schema_change='append_new_columns' handles new columns safely
  • Use --full-refresh to rebuild incremental tables from scratch
  • Set defaults in dbt_project.yml per folder; override per-model when needed

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

For tables with millions or billions of rows, full refreshes become impossible — too slow, too expensive. Incremental models are the answer. They're tricky to get right (subtle bugs around late data and updates), but mastering them is essential for any production dbt project.

When to go incremental

  • Table is large enough that dbt run takes more than 5-10 minutes
  • Data is mostly append-only (new events, new orders)
  • Old rows rarely change, or you can identify when they do
  • You can identify "what's new" with a column (timestamp, ID)

Anatomy of an incremental model

# models/marts/fct_events.sql
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns'
) }}

select
    event_id,
    user_id,
    event_type,
    event_ts,
    page_url,
    properties
from {{ ref('stg_events') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts > (select coalesce(max(event_ts), '2000-01-01') from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# Three critical pieces:
# 1. materialized='incremental'
# 2. unique_key (so dbt knows what to update vs insert)
# 3. is_incremental() block (filter for new data only)

The unique_key

Critical for the merge strategy. Tells dbt which rows in the existing table to update vs insert new:

# Single column unique key
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id'
) }}

# Composite unique key (more than one column)
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key=['user_id', 'event_ts']
) }}

# With dbt_utils surrogate key (recommended)
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_sk'
) }}

select
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['user_id', 'event_ts']) }} as event_sk,
    ...

The late-arriving data problem

Data sometimes arrives out of order. A naive incremental filter misses it:

# NAIVE — misses late data
{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts > (select max(event_ts) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# Problem: 
# Run at 2pm; max(event_ts) = 1:55pm
# At 2:05pm a webhook delivers an event timestamped 1:50pm
# Next run at 3pm: filter is event_ts > 2:55pm
# The 1:50pm event is MISSED forever

# SAFER — overlap window
{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts >= (select max(event_ts) - interval '3 days' from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

# Now we look back 3 days. Late data within that window gets picked up.
# unique_key + merge strategy ensures no duplicates.

The merge strategy in detail

# With incremental_strategy='merge', dbt generates SQL like:

# 1. Build new data into a temp table:
CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp_new_data AS
    SELECT * FROM stg_events
    WHERE event_ts >= (SELECT max(event_ts) - interval '3 days' FROM fct_events);

# 2. Merge into existing:
MERGE INTO fct_events AS target
USING tmp_new_data AS source
ON target.event_id = source.event_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ... 
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...;

# Result: updates existing rows by unique_key, inserts new rows

Backfilling and full refresh

# Force a full rebuild (drops + recreates table)
dbt run --select fct_events --full-refresh

# When to full-refresh:
# - You changed business logic
# - You added/changed columns
# - You suspect data integrity issues
# - You're testing changes in dev

# Backfill a specific date range (manual)
# Option 1: temporarily change is_incremental filter, run, revert
# Option 2: use dbt vars
{% if is_incremental() %}
  where event_ts BETWEEN '{{ var("backfill_start") }}'
                    AND '{{ var("backfill_end") }}'
{% endif %}

# Run with vars
dbt run --select fct_events --vars '{backfill_start: "2025-01-01", backfill_end: "2025-01-31"}'

Pre/post hooks for incremental

Sometimes you need to do extra work around the incremental run:

{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    pre_hook="DELETE FROM {{ this }} WHERE event_ts < current_date - 730",  -- archive old data
    post_hook="ALTER TABLE {{ this }} CLUSTER BY (event_ts)"  -- maintain clustering
) }}

# Pre-hook runs BEFORE the model SQL
# Post-hook runs AFTER

# Useful for:
# - Deleting old data (rolling windows)
# - Re-clustering / re-partitioning
# - Updating statistics
# - Notifying downstream systems

Avoiding duplicates: defensive patterns

# Pattern 1: dedup in the incremental SELECT
select * from (
    select 
        *,
        row_number() over (partition by event_id order by event_ts desc) as rn
    from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
    {% if is_incremental() %}
      where event_ts >= (select max(event_ts) - interval '3 days' from {{ this }})
    {% endif %}
) 
where rn = 1

# Pattern 2: test for duplicates after the fact
# In schema.yml:
- name: event_id
  tests:
    - unique
    - not_null

# Pattern 3: explicit MERGE behavior
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    merge_update_columns=['event_type', 'page_url', 'properties']  -- only update these on conflict
) }}

Snowflake-specific: clustering

# For Snowflake, cluster by columns you filter on:
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    cluster_by=['event_ts', 'event_type']
) }}

# dbt generates: CREATE TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (event_ts, event_type)
# Speeds up subsequent queries that filter on those columns

BigQuery-specific: partition + cluster

{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    incremental_strategy='insert_overwrite',
    partition_by={
        "field": "event_ts",
        "data_type": "timestamp",
        "granularity": "day"
    },
    cluster_by=['event_type']
) }}

# Best of both: daily partitions + event_type clustering
# Incremental overwrites only changed partitions
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an incremental model across two runs
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='event_id') }}

select event_id, user_id, event_type, event_ts
from {{ ref('stg_app__events') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- only rows newer than what this table already holds
  where event_ts > (select coalesce(max(event_ts), '1900-01-01') from {{ this }})
{% endif %}
$ python3 -c "import duckdb; print('fct_events rows:', duckdb.connect('warehouse.duckdb').sql('select count(*) from dev_natasha.fct_events').fetchone()[0])" fct_events rows: 100 $ python3 -c "import duckdb; c=duckdb.connect('warehouse.duckdb'); c.sql(\"insert into raw.events select i, 1 + i % 3, 'view', timestamp '2026-09-01 00:00' + interval (i) minute, now() from range(101, 121) t(i)\"); print('20 new raw events landed')" 20 new raw events landed $ dbt run --select fct_events 1 of 1 START sql incremental model dev_natasha.fct_events ...................... [RUN] 1 of 1 OK created sql incremental model dev_natasha.fct_events ................. [OK in 0.15s] Finished running 1 incremental model in 0 hours 0 minutes and 0.31 seconds (0.31s). Completed successfully Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1 $ cat target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/fct_events.sql select event_id, user_id, event_type, event_ts from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__events" -- only rows newer than what this table already holds where event_ts > (select coalesce(max(event_ts), '1900-01-01') from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."fct_events") $ python3 -c "import duckdb; print('fct_events rows:', duckdb.connect('warehouse.duckdb').sql('select count(*) from dev_natasha.fct_events').fetchone()[0])" fct_events rows: 120

Walk through it: after the first build the table holds 100 events. Twenty new raw events land. On the second run is_incremental() is true, so the compiled SQL carries the WHERE clause that reads only rows newer than the table's own maximum timestamp, and the table grows to 120 without touching the first 100. On the first run that clause was absent and the whole source was loaded. unique_key is what lets a re-delivered event replace its earlier copy instead of duplicating it.

▸ PRODUCTION-GRADE INCREMENTAL EVENTS MODEL
# models/marts/fct_user_events.sql
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_sk',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns',
    cluster_by=['event_ts', 'event_type']
) }}

with source as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_events') }}

    {% if is_incremental() %}
      -- 3-day overlap for late-arriving data
      where event_ts >= (select max(event_ts) - interval '3 days' from {{ this }})
    {% endif %}
),

deduped as (
    select 
        *,
        row_number() over (
            partition by event_id 
            order by event_ts desc, ingested_at desc
        ) as rn
    from source
),

final as (
    select
        {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['event_id']) }} as event_sk,
        event_id,
        user_id,
        event_type,
        event_ts,
        page_url,
        properties,
        ingested_at
    from deduped
    where rn = 1
)

select * from final

# Schema.yml:
# columns:
#   - name: event_sk
#     tests: [unique, not_null]
#   - name: event_id
#     tests: [not_null]
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Incremental: insert/merge only new rows instead of full rebuild
  • Critical config: materialized='incremental', unique_key, is_incremental() filter
  • Late-arriving data: use an overlap window (e.g., last 3 days)
  • Strategies: merge (default, handles updates), append, delete+insert, insert_overwrite
  • on_schema_change='append_new_columns' is the safe default
  • --full-refresh rebuilds from scratch (useful after logic changes)
  • Snowflake: add cluster_by for query speed
  • BigQuery: use partition_by + insert_overwrite strategy
  • Always test unique on the unique_key after building

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Source changes are localizedFivetran schema change?

Consistent naminganalyst doesn't need to remember which source called it email_address vs email .
Findableanyone can map a column in the warehouse back to its source.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Sources are the BOUNDARY between dbt and the outside world. Declaring them properly enables lineage tracking, freshness monitoring, and clean documentation. The staging convention (stg_) creates a stable interface between sources and your marts — protecting your business logic from source schema changes.

What sources are

A source in dbt is raw data loaded into your warehouse by an extract/load tool (Fivetran, Airbyte, etc.) — anything you didn't build with dbt.

# Declare sources in a YAML file (anywhere in models/)
# Convention: models/staging/<source>/_<source>__sources.yml

# models/staging/stripe/_stripe__sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: stripe                       ← logical name (used in {{ source() }})
    description: Stripe payment data via Fivetran
    database: raw                      ← warehouse database
    schema: stripe                     ← warehouse schema
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced  ← for freshness checks
    
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 12, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
    
    tables:
      - name: charges
        description: Successful charge events
        columns:
          - name: id
            description: Stripe charge ID
            tests: [unique, not_null]
          - name: amount
            description: Amount in cents
          - name: customer
            description: FK to stripe.customers
            tests:
              - relationships:
                  to: source('stripe', 'customers')
                  field: id
      
      - name: customers
        description: Stripe customer records
      
      - name: refunds
        description: Refund events

The source() function

# Reference a declared source:
select * from {{ source('stripe', 'charges') }}

# Compiles to:
select * from raw.stripe.charges

# If you later change schema:
# Update YAML once → all source() refs update automatically

Source freshness

Detect stale data automatically. If a source hasn't been updated recently, alert.

# In _stripe__sources.yml:
sources:
  - name: stripe
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced  ← timestamp column in the raw table
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 12, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}

# Run freshness check:
dbt source freshness

# Output:
# WARN  freshness for source.stripe.charges:
#   loaded 18 hours ago (warn threshold: 12 hours)
# 
# ERROR freshness for source.stripe.customers:
#   loaded 25 hours ago (error threshold: 24 hours)

# Use in CI to alert when extract pipelines fail.
# Period options: hour, day, minute

The staging layer convention

The first dbt layer: one staging model per source table. Naming: stg_<source>__<entity> (double underscore!).

# models/staging/stripe/stg_stripe__charges.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('stripe', 'charges') }}
),

renamed as (
    select
        -- IDs (string for safety)
        id              as charge_id,
        customer        as customer_id,
        
        -- Numerics (with unit conversion)
        amount / 100.0  as amount_usd,
        amount_refunded / 100.0 as amount_refunded_usd,
        
        -- Strings
        currency::text  as currency,
        status::text    as status,
        description::text as description,
        
        -- Timestamps
        created::timestamp as created_at,
        
        -- Booleans (cleaned)
        captured::boolean as is_captured,
        refunded::boolean as is_refunded
    
    from source
    where _fivetran_deleted is null   -- exclude soft-deleted rows
)

select * from renamed

What staging does (and doesn't)

DO in staging DON'T in staging
Rename columns to consistent style JOIN to other tables
Cast types explicitly Apply business logic
Unit conversions (cents → dollars) Aggregate or summarize
Drop columns you'll never use Pivot or reshape
Filter out test/deleted rows Compute derived metrics
Add simple flags (is_X from status) Implement segmentation logic

Naming conventions

# Column naming:
# - snake_case
# - descriptive (customer_id, not cust_id)
# - units in name when ambiguous (amount_usd, duration_sec)

# IDs:
# - foreign keys: <entity>_id (customer_id, product_id)
# - if you create a surrogate key: <entity>_sk

# Timestamps:
# - ending in _at: created_at, updated_at, signed_up_at
# - or _ts for raw timestamps: event_ts

# Dates:
# - ending in _date: order_date, signup_date

# Booleans:
# - is_X: is_active, is_premium
# - has_X: has_subscription
# - was_X: was_refunded

# Status fields:
# - status, state, type (singular)

Why this discipline matters

  • Source changes are localized — Fivetran schema change? Only the stg_ model breaks.
  • Marts query staging, not sources — clean interface.
  • Consistent naming — analyst doesn't need to remember which source called it email_address vs email.
  • Findable — anyone can map a column in the warehouse back to its source.

Documenting sources

# Full source documentation
sources:
  - name: stripe
    description: |
      Stripe payment data extracted by Fivetran every hour.
      Owner: data-platform-team
      Documentation: https://wiki/internal/data-sources/stripe
    
    database: raw
    schema: stripe
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced
    
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 2, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
    
    tables:
      - name: charges
        description: |
          Each successful charge event. Customers may have multiple charges
          (one per invoice). Refunds are tracked in stripe.refunds.
        loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced
        columns:
          - name: id
            description: Stripe-provided charge ID (string)
            tests: [unique, not_null]
          - name: amount
            description: Amount in cents (integer)
          - name: customer
            description: Stripe customer ID
            tests:
              - relationships:
                  to: source('stripe', 'customers')
                  field: id

Codegen for boilerplate

The dbt-labs/codegen package generates source declarations and staging models automatically:

# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/codegen
    version: 0.12.0

# Generate source YAML for a schema:
dbt run-operation generate_source --args '{schema_name: stripe, database_name: raw}'

# Generate base staging model SQL:
dbt run-operation generate_base_model --args '{source_name: stripe, table_name: charges}'

# Saves typing for projects with many tables
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — declared sources, and a freshness check that catches a stale one
version: 2
sources:
  - name: app
    description: The team's application database, replicated hourly
    schema: raw
    loaded_at_field: _loaded_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 12, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
    tables:
      - name: orders
      - name: customers
      - name: events
$ dbt source freshness 1 of 3 START freshness of app.customers ........................................ [RUN] 2 of 3 START freshness of app.events ........................................... [RUN] 3 of 3 START freshness of app.orders ........................................... [RUN] 1 of 3 ERROR STALE freshness of app.customers .................................. [ERROR STALE in 0.06s] 3 of 3 PASS freshness of app.orders ............................................ [PASS in 0.06s] 2 of 3 PASS freshness of app.events ............................................ [PASS in 0.06s] Finished running 3 sources in 0 hours 0 minutes and 0.23 seconds (0.23s). [ERROR]: in source customers (models/staging/app/_app__sources.yml) Status: error Done.
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: the YAML declares the app source once: its schema, the column that says when each row was loaded, and how old is too old. dbt source freshness then checks every table: orders and events were loaded two hours ago and pass; customers was last loaded thirty hours ago, past the 24-hour error threshold, and is reported ERROR STALE before any model built on it can mislead a dashboard.

▸ COMPLETE STAGING MODEL WITH DOCS
# models/staging/stripe/_stripe__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: stg_stripe__charges
    description: |
      Cleaned and renamed view of Stripe charges.
      Filters out soft-deleted rows. Converts amounts to USD.
    columns:
      - name: charge_id
        description: Stripe charge identifier
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_id
        description: FK to stg_stripe__customers
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('stg_stripe__customers')
              field: customer_id
      - name: amount_usd
        description: Charge amount in USD (converted from cents)
      - name: is_captured
        description: Whether the charge was successfully captured
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: [true, false]
      - name: created_at
        description: Charge creation timestamp (UTC)
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Sources = raw data loaded by extract/load tools (not built by dbt)
  • Declare in YAML with database, schema, tables
  • Reference via {{ source('schema', 'table') }}
  • Freshness checks: dbt source freshness alerts on stale data
  • Staging convention: stg_<source>__<entity> (double underscore)
  • Staging does light cleanup only — no JOINs, no business logic
  • Staging creates stable interface between sources and marts
  • codegen package automates source YAML and staging boilerplate
  • Document sources thoroughly — they're the boundary of your project

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
uniqueno duplicate values in a column
accepted_valuesonly allowed enum values
relationshipsall values exist in another model's column
Tests on sourcesyes — the SAME test syntax (unique, not_null, accepted_values) applies in sources.yml, guarding raw inputs before any model runs.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The four built-in dbt tests — unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships — catch 80% of data quality issues with one line of YAML. They're declarative, run in CI, and protect your dashboards from silent bugs. Skipping them is the #1 reason data teams find issues in production rather than catching them in development.

The four generic tests

DBT'S BUILT-IN TESTS
unique: no duplicate values in a column
not_null: no NULL values
accepted_values: only allowed enum values
relationships: all values exist in another model's column

Declaring tests in schema.yml

# models/marts/_marts__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: One row per completed order
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: Primary key
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      
      - name: customer_id
        description: FK to dim_customers
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_customers')
              field: customer_id
      
      - name: status
        description: Order status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['pending', 'completed', 'cancelled', 'refunded']
      
      - name: amount_usd
        description: Order total in USD
        tests:
          - not_null

Running tests

# Run ALL tests
dbt test

# Run tests for one model
dbt test --select fct_orders

# Run tests for a model AND all its dependencies
dbt test --select +fct_orders

# Run only failures from previous run (after fixing)
dbt test --select result:fail --state ./target_prev

# Build (run + test in dependency order)
dbt build --select fct_orders+

# Output:
# PASS unique_fct_orders_order_id ............................. [PASS in 1.2s]
# PASS not_null_fct_orders_order_id ........................... [PASS in 0.8s]
# FAIL accepted_values_fct_orders_status ..................... [FAIL 3 in 1.5s]
# Got 3 results, configured to fail if != 0

How tests work under the hood

Every test compiles to a SELECT query. If the query returns rows, the test FAILS. If it returns zero rows, the test PASSES.

# YAML test:
- name: order_id
  tests:
    - unique

# Compiles to:
select order_id from fct_orders
group by order_id
having count(*) > 1

# Returns rows = duplicates exist = test fails
# Returns 0 rows = all unique = test passes

# unique test compiled SQL:
select order_id, count(*) as n
from fct_orders
where order_id is not null
group by 1
having count(*) > 1

# not_null compiled SQL:
select * from fct_orders where order_id is null

# accepted_values:
select status from fct_orders
where status not in ('pending', 'completed', 'cancelled', 'refunded')

# relationships:
select customer_id from fct_orders
where customer_id is not null
  and customer_id not in (select customer_id from dim_customers)

The relationships test (deep dive)

The most important test for data integrity. Verifies every foreign key points to a real row in the referenced table:

# Critical for catching orphan foreign keys
- name: customer_id
  tests:
    - relationships:
        to: ref('dim_customers')         ← which model
        field: customer_id               ← which column
        # Optional: where filter
        where: "is_active = true"

# Will catch:
# - dim_customers rebuilt with fewer rows (data loss)
# - New fct_orders customer_id that doesn't exist in dim_customers
# - Schema drift (column rename in dim that fact still references)

accepted_values for enums

# Lock down expected values
- name: customer_segment
  tests:
    - accepted_values:
        values: ['enterprise', 'mid_market', 'smb', 'individual']

# If marketing adds a new segment 'startup' without telling data team:
# Next run FAILS with the unknown value
# Forces a conversation before silent breakage

Configuring tests

# Make a test only warn (don't error)
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - not_null:
        severity: warn

# Test with where clause (test only some rows)
- name: customer_id
  tests:
    - relationships:
        to: ref('dim_customers')
        field: customer_id
        where: "is_completed = true"     ← only test completed orders

# Test names (so it's easier to find failures)
- name: order_id
  tests:
    - unique:
        name: orders_have_unique_ids
    - not_null

# Run tests in groups (tags)
- name: order_id
  tests:
    - unique:
        config:
          tags: ['critical']

# Run only tagged tests
dbt test --select tag:critical

Tests at the model level (not just column)

# Test combinations of columns (composite unique key)
models:
  - name: fct_order_items
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns: [order_id, line_item_id]
    columns:
      ...

# Equality test (two models should have same rows)
- name: fct_orders_v2
  tests:
    - dbt_utils.equality:
        compare_model: ref('fct_orders_v1')

dbt_utils tests

The dbt-labs/dbt_utils package adds many additional tests:

# Install via packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.1.1

# Useful tests:

# Composite unique key
- dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
    combination_of_columns: [user_id, event_ts]

# Expression test (any SQL expression)
- dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
    expression: "amount_usd >= 0"

# Cardinality (foreign key equality of values)
- dbt_utils.cardinality_equality:
    field: customer_id
    to: ref('dim_customers')

# Recency (most recent row within X days)
- dbt_utils.recency:
    datepart: day
    field: event_ts
    interval: 1

# At least one row
- dbt_utils.at_least_one

# Empty string vs NULL check
- dbt_utils.not_empty_string

dbt_expectations (advanced)

Inspired by Great Expectations. Many more test types:

packages:
  - package: calogica/dbt_expectations
    version: 0.10.4

# Examples:
- dbt_expectations.expect_column_values_to_be_between:
    column: amount_usd
    min_value: 0
    max_value: 1000000

- dbt_expectations.expect_column_value_lengths_to_be_between:
    column: email
    min_value: 5
    max_value: 100

- dbt_expectations.expect_row_values_to_have_data_for_every_n_datepart:
    date_col: order_date
    date_part: day
    test_start_date: '2025-01-01'

Severity and failure modes

# Default: severity=error (fail the run)
# Optional: severity=warn (warn but continue)

# Set error threshold for warnings
- dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
    expression: "amount_usd >= 0"
    config:
      severity: warn
      warn_if: "> 10"            ← warn if more than 10 rows fail
      error_if: "> 100"          ← error if more than 100 rows fail

# Useful for "tolerable amounts of bad data"

Test best practices

  • Minimum tests for every model: unique + not_null on PK; not_null + relationships on FKs
  • Always test grain key — composite tests for composite grains
  • Test status fields with accepted_values — catches new enum values
  • Test source data too — early failure beats deep debugging
  • Run dbt build, not just dbt run — tests gate the next downstream model
  • Tests in CI are mandatory — never merge a PR that fails tests

version: 2
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: One row per order, in dollars, joined to the customer's segment.
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: Primary key of the order.
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - relationships:
              arguments:
                to: ref('dim_customers')

          - accepted_values:

      - name: amount_usd
        tests:
          - assert_positive_value
  - name: dim_customers
    description: One row per customer.
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        tests: [unique, not_null]

▸ COMPLETE FCT_ORDERS WITH TESTS
# models/marts/_marts__models.yml

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: |
      Order-level fact table. Grain: one row per completed order.
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
          expression: "amount_usd >= 0"
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: Primary key
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      
      - name: customer_id
        description: FK to dim_customers
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_customers')
              field: customer_id
      
      - name: product_id
        description: FK to dim_products
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_products')
              field: product_id
      
      - name: status
        tests:
          - not_null
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['completed']    ← marts only have completed orders
      
      - name: amount_usd
        tests:
          - not_null
          - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
              expression: ">= 0"
      
      - name: order_date
        tests:
          - not_null
          - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
              expression: "<= current_date"
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Four built-in tests: unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships
  • Tests are SQL: return rows = fail; return 0 rows = pass
  • Always test PKs with unique + not_null
  • Always test FKs with not_null + relationships
  • Test enums with accepted_values (catches new values)
  • severity: warn vs error (default)
  • dbt_utils adds composite keys, expressions, cardinality tests
  • dbt_expectations adds value-range, length, recency tests
  • Run dbt build (run + test) instead of dbt run alone
  • Tests in CI are mandatory; never merge with failing tests

Tests on sources: yes — the SAME test syntax (unique, not_null, accepted_values) applies in sources.yml, guarding raw inputs before any model runs.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Generic tests cover 80% of cases. The remaining 20% — business rules, complex relationships, cross-table consistency — need custom tests. Knowing how to write them turns dbt from a "schema enforcer" into a true data-quality framework.

Singular tests

A singular test is a one-off SQL query in the tests/ folder. If it returns rows, the test fails.

# tests/assert_revenue_positive.sql
-- Test: no order has negative revenue
SELECT *
FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
WHERE amount_usd < 0

# Returns rows = fail. Returns 0 = pass.
# That's it. Just SQL that finds bad data.

# Run with the rest:
dbt test
# Or specifically:
dbt test --select assert_revenue_positive

When to use singular tests

  • One-off business rule (not reused)
  • Complex multi-table consistency check
  • Test against external systems or sources
  • Quick "did this thing happen?" check

Examples of useful singular tests

# tests/assert_dim_customers_complete.sql
-- Every customer in fct_orders should exist in dim_customers
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }} o
LEFT JOIN {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c USING (customer_id)
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL

# tests/assert_monthly_revenue_matches.sql
-- Revenue calculated two ways should match
WITH from_orders AS (
    SELECT 
        date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month,
        SUM(amount_usd) AS rev
    FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
    GROUP BY 1
),
from_aggregate AS (
    SELECT month, revenue AS rev
    FROM {{ ref('fct_monthly_metrics') }}
)
SELECT o.month, o.rev AS from_orders, a.rev AS from_metrics
FROM from_orders o
JOIN from_aggregate a USING (month)
WHERE ABS(o.rev - a.rev) > 0.01     -- tolerate small float diffs

# tests/assert_no_future_orders.sql
SELECT *
FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
WHERE order_date > current_date

# tests/assert_active_users_have_signup.sql
SELECT u.user_id
FROM {{ ref('dim_users') }} u
WHERE u.is_active = true
  AND u.signup_date IS NULL

Custom generic tests

When you find yourself copy-pasting the same singular test logic, turn it into a generic test — a parameterized test you can declare in YAML.

# Define in tests/generic/ or macros/

# tests/generic/assert_positive_value.sql
{% test assert_positive_value(model, column_name) %}

SELECT *
FROM {{ model }}
WHERE {{ column_name }} < 0

{% endtest %}

# Now use in YAML:
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - assert_positive_value

# Or with explicit syntax:
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - assert_positive_value:
        column_name: amount_usd

Generic test with arguments

# tests/generic/test_max_value.sql
{% test max_value(model, column_name, max_value) %}

SELECT *
FROM {{ model }}
WHERE {{ column_name }} > {{ max_value }}

{% endtest %}

# YAML:
- name: discount_pct
  tests:
    - max_value:
        max_value: 100

Severity and thresholds

# Allow some failures, error only above threshold
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - not_null:
        config:
          severity: warn
          warn_if: "> 5"        ← warn if more than 5 nulls
          error_if: "> 100"     ← error if more than 100

# In singular tests:
{{ config(
    severity='warn',
    warn_if='> 0',
    error_if='> 10'
) }}

SELECT * FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }} WHERE amount_usd < 0

Inline column tests

# Inline expression test (no need for separate file)
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
        expression: ">= 0 AND <= 1000000"

# Use the model variable too:
- name: amount_usd
  tests:
    - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
        expression: "{{ column_name }} = price * quantity"

The dbt-labs/dbt_utils package tests

Test Use case
unique_combination_of_columns Composite primary keys
expression_is_true Any SQL boolean expression
recency Most-recent row is within N days
cardinality_equality Same set of values in two columns
at_least_one At least one non-null row exists
not_empty_string No empty strings (in addition to NULLs)
equality Two models have same rows

Cross-table consistency tests

# Test that aggregate matches source
# tests/assert_orders_match_charges.sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT SUM(amount_usd) AS total FROM {{ ref('fct_orders') }} 
    WHERE status = 'completed'
),
charge_totals AS (
    SELECT SUM(amount_usd) AS total FROM {{ ref('stg_stripe__charges') }} 
    WHERE is_captured = true
)
SELECT 
    o.total AS orders_total,
    c.total AS charges_total,
    ABS(o.total - c.total) AS diff
FROM order_totals o, charge_totals c
WHERE ABS(o.total - c.total) > 100   -- tolerate small reconciliation diffs

Auditing data quality over time

# Store test results for trending
# dbt_project.yml:
on-run-end:
  - "{% do log('All tests done!', info=true) %}"

# Or use packages:
# - elementary-data/elementary (test result history + alerting)
# - dbt-labs/dbt_artifacts (parse manifest.json + run_results.json)

# Output:
# - Dashboards showing test pass rates over time
# - Slack alerts on critical test failures
# - Trend detection (e.g., null rate rising)
★ TESTING STRATEGY BY LAYER
  • Sources: source freshness, row count bounds
  • Staging: unique on PK, not_null on key columns, accepted_values on enums
  • Intermediate: consistency between joined sources
  • Marts: unique on grain key, relationships on FKs, business-rule expressions
  • Cross-mart: singular tests checking metric consistency

Walk through it: a singular test is a SELECT that returns the rows that are wrong: here, orders with negative revenue. A custom generic test is the same idea with parameters: assert_positive_value takes any model and column, and the YAML applies it to amount_usd in one line. ▸ REAL-WORLD TEST SUITE FOR A MART
# models/marts/_finance__models.yml

models:
  - name: fct_subscription_periods
    description: One row per (subscription, month). MRR analysis.
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns: [subscription_id, year_month]
      - dbt_utils.expression_is_true:
          expression: "mrr_usd >= 0"
      - dbt_utils.recency:
          datepart: month
          field: year_month
          interval: 1
    columns:
      - name: subscription_id
        tests:
          - not_null
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_customers')
              field: customer_id
      - name: year_month
        tests:
          - not_null
      - name: plan
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['free', 'starter', 'pro', 'enterprise']
      - name: mrr_usd
        tests:
          - not_null

# tests/assert_active_subs_have_mrr.sql
SELECT *
FROM {{ ref('fct_subscription_periods') }}
WHERE is_active = true AND mrr_usd <= 0
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Singular tests = one-off SQL queries in tests/ folder
  • Generic tests = parameterized, reusable tests in tests/generic/
  • SQL pattern: return rows = fail; return 0 rows = pass
  • dbt_utils provides composite keys, expressions, recency, equality tests
  • dbt_expectations adds value bounds, length, frequency tests
  • severity: warn vs error; warn_if/error_if thresholds for tolerable failures
  • Test strategy by layer: source freshness, staging keys, mart relationships, cross-mart consistency
  • Elementary or dbt_artifacts packages track test history over time
