◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Data without docs is useless. A new analyst joining the team sees thousands of columns named cryptically — amt_usd_g_net, flag_xy, ts_mod — and has no idea what they mean. Documentation is the difference between "the data team is a black box" and "anyone can self-serve." dbt's built-in docs system makes this nearly automatic: write descriptions in YAML; dbt generates a beautiful searchable website. The CR-DBT exam tests both the syntax and the dbt-specific commands.

Where docs live in dbt

Documentation lives in YAML files alongside your models. Each model gets a description, and each column does too.

# models/marts/dim_customers.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: dim_customers
    description: "One row per customer. Built daily from raw CRM data."
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        description: "Surrogate key. Unique. Never recycled."
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: email
        description: "Primary email address. Lowercased and trimmed."
        tests:
          - not_null
      - name: signup_date
        description: "Date the customer first registered. UTC."
      - name: lifetime_value
        description: "Cumulative gross revenue in USD. Refreshed nightly."

Save the file and dbt picks it up automatically. The descriptions show up in:

  • The dbt docs site (next section)
  • Other tools that import dbt manifests (Hightouch, Lightdash, etc.)
  • Some IDE plugins, on hover

Generating the docs site

# Generate docs (compiles project + introspects warehouse)
dbt docs generate

# Serve them on localhost
dbt docs serve
# Opens http://localhost:8080 in your browser

The generated site includes:

  • Every model, source, seed, snapshot
  • Descriptions for models and columns
  • Column-level data types (introspected from the warehouse)
  • Test definitions and status
  • The compiled SQL for each model
  • A searchable directory and a LINEAGE GRAPH

The lineage graph (DAG)

The lineage graph is the killer feature. It shows every model as a node, every ref() as an edge:

source.crm.customers ─→ stg_customers ─→ dim_customers ─→ fct_revenue
                                                       ↘  rpt_kpis
source.shopify.orders ─→ stg_orders ─→ fct_orders ────→ fct_revenue

Click any model to see its upstream sources and downstream consumers. Critical for impact analysis: "If I change stg_orders, what breaks?"

Writing good descriptions

Bad:

description: "Customer table"

Good:

description: |
  One row per customer. Built daily at 04:00 UTC from raw CRM data.
  
  - Grain: customer_id
  - Refresh cadence: daily
  - Source of truth: Salesforce (via Fivetran)
  - Owner: data-platform@company.com
  
  Caveats:
  - Includes test accounts (filter on is_test_account = false)
  - Excludes deleted customers; historical IDs available in dim_customers_archive

Note the YAML multiline string (|). Each description should answer:

  • What's the grain? (one row per WHAT)
  • How often does it refresh?
  • Where does the data come from?
  • Who owns it?
  • Any caveats, exclusions, or known issues

Column descriptions

Each column should describe:

  • What it represents (in business terms)
  • Units (USD, count, percentage)
  • Any transformations (lowercased, rounded, multiplied)
  • Nullability and meaning of null
columns:
  - name: amt_usd
    description: "Order total in USD, including tax, excluding shipping. Null if the order was canceled."
  - name: country_iso2
    description: "Customer's country, ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 (e.g., 'US', 'GB'). Uppercase. Null for guest checkout."

Reusable docs blocks

For descriptions you reuse across models (e.g., customer_id appears in 20 tables), define a doc block once:

# models/docs.md
{% docs customer_id %}
Surrogate key for the customer dimension. Generated by hash of raw CRM `email` (lowercased + trimmed) at ingestion. Stable across refreshes.
{% enddocs %}

Reference it from YAML:

columns:
  - name: customer_id
    description: "{{ doc('customer_id') }}"

Update the doc block once; all references update automatically.

Source docs

Don't forget to document your sources too:

sources:
  - name: crm
    database: raw
    schema: salesforce
    description: "Salesforce export via Fivetran, refreshed hourly."
    tables:
      - name: customers
        description: "Raw customer records from Salesforce Contact object."
        columns:
          - name: id
            description: "Salesforce Contact Id (18 chars, case-sensitive)."

Tests are documentation

Tests aren't just for catching bugs — they also DOCUMENT expectations:

columns:
  - name: status
    description: "Order status."
    tests:
      - accepted_values:
          values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled']

Someone reading the YAML knows EXACTLY what values to expect — and dbt enforces it on every run.

Hosting docs for the team

Three options:

  1. dbt Cloud — auto-generates and hosts docs at https://yourcompany.dbtcloud.com/docs
  2. Self-hosted — run dbt docs generate in CI, push the output to S3 / GCS / Netlify behind your SSO
  3. dbt-docs in a Docker container — slightly more setup

Most teams set up CI to regenerate docs on every PR merge. Stale docs are nearly as bad as no docs.

Beyond dbt docs

dbt's docs are great but not always enough. Mature teams pair them with:

  • A data catalog (Atlan, DataHub, Castor) for cross-source lineage and search
  • A BI semantic layer (LookML, dbt Semantic Layer) for metric definitions
  • An exposures section in dbt documenting downstream dashboards and reports

The exposures system

exposures:
  - name: weekly_kpi_dashboard
    type: dashboard
    url: https://looker.company.com/dashboards/42
    description: "Executive KPI dashboard — reviewed weekly."
    depends_on:
      - ref('rpt_kpis')
    owner:
      name: Data Platform Team
      email: data-platform@company.com

Exposures show up in the lineage graph as DOWNSTREAM consumers. Now you can answer "if I change rpt_kpis, what dashboards break?"

Walk through it: dbt docs generate compiles the project, inspects the warehouse for column types, and writes catalog.json next to manifest.json. The manifest is the same information the docs site renders: the description written in YAML, the column descriptions, and the upstream dependencies. dbt docs serve turns those two files into the browsable site with the lineage graph.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Documentation lives in YAML files alongside models; descriptions for both models and columns
  • dbt docs generate compiles a searchable docs site; dbt docs serve opens it locally
  • Good model descriptions answer: grain, refresh cadence, source, owner, caveats
  • Good column descriptions answer: what it represents, units, transformations, nullability
  • Multiline YAML descriptions use the | indicator
  • Reusable doc blocks ({% docs name %}...{% enddocs %}) avoid duplication; reference with {{ doc('name') }}
  • Document SOURCES too — not just final marts
  • Tests like accepted_values double as enforced documentation
  • The lineage graph (DAG) is the killer feature for impact analysis
  • Use the exposures system to document downstream consumers (dashboards, ML pipelines)

Sources can fail silently. Fivetran misses a sync; a webhook lags; a database replica falls behind. Exposures track who downstream depends on your data. Source freshness checks alert you BEFORE consumers report wrong numbers. Both close important gaps in operational data quality.

Source freshness — declarative monitoring

# In sources YAML:
sources:
  - name: stripe
    database: raw
    schema: stripe
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced   ← timestamp Fivetran sets when it loads
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 1, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
    
    tables:
      - name: charges
        # Can override per-table
        freshness:
          warn_after: {count: 30, period: minute}
          error_after: {count: 2, period: hour}
      - name: customers
        # Inherits source-level freshness

# 12:30:02  WARN  freshness of stripe.charges ............. [WARN in 0.5s]
# 12:30:02  ERROR freshness of stripe.refunds ............. [ERROR in 0.4s]

# - When each table was last loaded

What exposures are

An exposure declares a downstream consumer of dbt models — a dashboard, a notebook, a ML model, an application. Tracks the dependency for documentation and impact analysis.

# models/exposures/_exposures.yml
version: 2

exposures:
  - name: weekly_business_review
    type: dashboard                    ← dashboard, notebook, ml, application
    maturity: high                     ← high, medium, low
    description: |
      The CEO's weekly metrics dashboard. Powers the leadership team's
      Monday standup. Mission-critical.
    url: https://looker.company.com/dashboards/47
    
    owner:
      name: Sarah Smith
      email: sarah@company.com
    
    depends_on:
      - ref('fct_orders')
      - ref('fct_subscription_periods')
      - ref('dim_customers')
      - ref('fct_marketing_attribution')
    
    tags: ['executive', 'weekly']
  
  - name: customer_health_score_model
    type: ml
    maturity: medium
    description: ML model predicting churn risk per customer
    url: https://mlflow.company.com/experiments/health-score
    owner:
      name: Data Science Team
      email: ds@company.com
    depends_on:
      - ref('dim_customers')
      - ref('fct_subscription_periods')
      - ref('fct_support_tickets')
    
  - name: marketing_attribution_app
    type: application
    description: Internal app showing attribution dashboard
    url: https://marketing.company.com
    depends_on:
      - ref('fct_marketing_attribution')

Why exposures matter

  1. Lineage to consumers — see who depends on each model
  2. Impact analysis — before changing a model, check what breaks
  3. Ownership tracking — who do I notify if this changes?
  4. Maturity signaling — mature exposures need more care
  5. Run-targeted selection — dbt build --select +exposure:dashboard_name

Selecting models by exposure

# Build all models needed for a specific dashboard
dbt build --select +exposure:weekly_business_review

# Builds everything upstream of that exposure
# Useful for "rebuild what the CEO needs to see"

# All exposures of a given type
dbt list --select exposure:type:dashboard

# All "high maturity" exposures (mission-critical)
dbt list --select exposure:maturity:high

Exposures in dbt docs

Exposures appear in the lineage graph as terminal nodes. Hovering shows owner, description, link. Anyone can navigate from a fact table to "who consumes this?"

Tracking expected vs actual

# Find models that have no downstream exposure
# (Potentially unused / orphan models)
dbt list --select +exposure:* --output json

# Compare to all models:
dbt list --output json

# The difference = models with no declared downstream consumer
# Often candidates for deprecation

Source freshness + exposures + CI

# Production schedule (e.g., hourly):
1. dbt source freshness                  ← detect stale sources
2. If any ERROR: alert + skip downstream
3. dbt build --select state:modified+    ← rebuild changed models
4. dbt source freshness --select +exposure:weekly_business_review
   (focused freshness check on CEO-critical sources)

# This pattern:
# - Catches source issues BEFORE downstream tables get stale
# - Focused checks on what matters most
# - Skips wasteful runs when sources haven't updated

Maturity levels

low Experimental, in development; failure expected
medium Used regularly by internal team; some monitoring
high Mission-critical; alerts, on-call, strict SLA
★ TIER YOUR TESTS BY EXPOSURE MATURITY

Mission-critical exposures deserve aggressive tests (recency, freshness, business-rule expressions). Experimental exposures can run with looser checks. Use exposures to prioritize quality investment.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Jinja is what turns dbt from "SQL with refs" into "SQL with superpowers." It lets you loop, branch, and parameterize SQL — eliminating repetitive code and enabling patterns impossible in plain SQL. Once Jinja clicks, your code becomes dramatically shorter and more maintainable.

What Jinja is

Jinja is a Python-style templating language. dbt uses it to extend SQL with variables, control flow, and reusable functions. Anything in {{ }} (expressions) or {% %} (statements) is Jinja.

TWO JINJA SYNTAXES
{{ expression }} — outputs a value (variable, function call, ref)
{% statement %} — control flow (if, for, set, macro)

Jinja runs FIRST, producing plain SQL. The warehouse never sees Jinja.

Variables: {{ var() }} and {{ env_var() }}

# In dbt_project.yml:
vars:
  start_date: '2020-01-01'
  exclude_test_data: true

# In a model:
select *
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where order_date >= '{{ var("start_date") }}'

{% if var('exclude_test_data') %}
  and customer_id != 'TEST'
{% endif %}

# Override at runtime:
dbt run --vars 'start_date: 2025-01-01'

{% if %} — conditional SQL

# Different logic per environment using target.name
select *
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
{% if target.name == 'prod' %}
  where order_date >= '2020-01-01'
{% else %}
  -- limit data in dev for speed
  where order_date >= current_date - 7
{% endif %}

# Build different columns conditionally:
select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    {% if target.name == 'prod' %}
        amount as amount_usd
    {% else %}
        round(amount, 2) as amount_usd
    {% endif %}
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

{% for %} — loops

The most useful Jinja pattern. Generate repetitive SQL from a list:

# Pivot example — without Jinja, this is 8 ugly lines:
select
    customer_id,
    sum(case when product = 'A' then amount end) as amount_a,
    sum(case when product = 'B' then amount end) as amount_b,
    sum(case when product = 'C' then amount end) as amount_c,
    sum(case when product = 'D' then amount end) as amount_d
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
group by 1

# With Jinja loop:
{% set products = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'] %}

select
    customer_id,
    {% for p in products %}
    sum(case when product = '{{ p }}' then amount end) as amount_{{ p | lower }}
    {{ ',' if not loop.last }}
    {% endfor %}
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
group by 1

# Now adding a 5th product = adding one item to the list.

{% set %} — set variables

# Define lists and values inline
{% set high_value_threshold = 1000 %}
{% set excluded_segments = ['internal', 'test'] %}

select
    order_id,
    case when amount >= {{ high_value_threshold }} 
         then 'high' else 'normal' end as tier
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where segment not in (
    {% for s in excluded_segments %}
    '{{ s }}'{{ ',' if not loop.last }}
    {% endfor %}
)

Whitespace control

Jinja's whitespace handling is finicky. Use - inside {%- or -%} to trim whitespace:

# Without whitespace control:
{% for p in products %}
  case when product = '{{ p }}' then amount end as amount_{{ p }}
  {{ ',' if not loop.last }}
{% endfor %}

# Compiles to ugly SQL with extra blank lines

# With whitespace control:
{%- for p in products -%}
  case when product = '{{ p }}' then amount end as amount_{{ p }}
  {{- ',' if not loop.last -}}
{%- endfor -%}

# Compiles to clean SQL — important for readability of target/compiled/

The {{ log() }} function — debugging

# Print Jinja values to the dbt log during compilation
{% set my_list = ['A', 'B', 'C'] %}
{{ log('my_list = ' ~ my_list, info=True) }}

# Run and see the output:
# dbt run
# 14:23:01 my_list = ['A', 'B', 'C']

# Essential for debugging Jinja logic

Inspecting compiled SQL is the secret weapon

When Jinja confuses you, look at target/compiled/<project>/path/to/model.sql. That's exactly what was sent to the warehouse — all Jinja resolved. Compare to your source SQL to see what each piece compiled to.

# Force compile without running:
dbt compile --select my_model

# Then check target/compiled/<project>/models/my_model.sql

Common Jinja gotchas

  • Quotes matter — string values must be quoted: '{{ var("x") }}' not {{ var("x") }}
  • Numbers vs strings — {{ 5 }} outputs 5 (number), {{ "5" }} outputs 5 (string)
  • Whitespace — extra blanks can break SQL if commas land in odd places
  • Trailing commas — use {{ ',' if not loop.last }} to avoid SQL syntax errors
  • Filters — | upper, | lower, | trim transform values
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a for-loop that writes the pivot for you
$ cat models/marts/rpt_product_pivot.sql; echo; echo '-- compiles to:'; cat target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/rpt_product_pivot.sql select customer_id {% for p in var('products') %} , sum(case when product = '{{ p }}' then amount_usd else 0 end) as amount_{{ p | lower }} {% endfor %} from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} group by 1 -- compiles to: select customer_id , sum(case when product = 'A' then amount_usd else 0 end) as amount_a , sum(case when product = 'B' then amount_usd else 0 end) as amount_b , sum(case when product = 'C' then amount_usd else 0 end) as amount_c from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."fct_orders" group by 1
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: the products live in a project variable. The loop emits one sum(case when ...) column per product, and the compiled SQL is exactly what you would have typed by hand, three times. Add a product to the variable and the report grows a column with no SQL edit. The blank lines in the compiled output are the loop's whitespace; {%- and -%} trim them if they bother you.

▸ A REAL JINJA REFACTOR
# Before — repetitive SQL, fragile:
select
    order_id,
    case when status = 'pending' then 1 else 0 end as is_pending,
    case when status = 'paid' then 1 else 0 end as is_paid,
    case when status = 'shipped' then 1 else 0 end as is_shipped,
    case when status = 'delivered' then 1 else 0 end as is_delivered,
    case when status = 'cancelled' then 1 else 0 end as is_cancelled,
    case when status = 'refunded' then 1 else 0 end as is_refunded
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# After — DRY, easy to extend:
{% set statuses = ['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled', 'refunded'] %}

select
    order_id,
    {% for s in statuses %}
    case when status = '{{ s }}' then 1 else 0 end as is_{{ s }}
    {{- ',' if not loop.last }}
    {% endfor %}
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# Adding a new status = adding one item to the list. No SQL changes.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Jinja = templating layer that runs before SQL
  • {{ expression }} outputs values; {% statement %} control flow
  • {{ var() }} reads from dbt_project.yml vars
  • {% if %} for conditional SQL (great with target.name)
  • {% for %} loops for DRY repetitive SQL
  • {% set %} for inline lists and variables
  • Use {%- and -%} for whitespace control
  • {{ log() }} for debugging
  • Always inspect target/compiled/ to see what compiled

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Macros are dbt's functions. They let you bottle up reusable SQL patterns and call them everywhere. Used right, they're the difference between a clean dbt project and one full of copy-pasted SQL drift. Every mature dbt project has its own macros library.

What a macro is

A macro is a reusable chunk of SQL or Jinja, defined in macros/ and callable from anywhere. Think Python functions — but they output SQL.

# macros/cents_to_dollars.sql
{% macro cents_to_dollars(column_name) %}
    {{ column_name }} / 100.0
{% endmacro %}

# Call from any model:
select
    order_id,
    {{ cents_to_dollars('amount_cents') }} as amount_usd
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# Compiles to:
select
    order_id,
    amount_cents / 100.0 as amount_usd
from analytics.stg_orders

Macros with multiple args

# macros/safe_divide.sql
{% macro safe_divide(numerator, denominator, default_value=0) %}
    case 
        when {{ denominator }} = 0 then {{ default_value }}
        else {{ numerator }}::numeric / {{ denominator }}
    end
{% endmacro %}

# Use:
select
    department_id,
    {{ safe_divide('total_revenue', 'order_count') }} as avg_order_value,
    {{ safe_divide('refunds', 'total_revenue', default_value='null') }} as refund_rate
from {{ ref('int_dept_metrics') }}

Macros that return SQL fragments

The most common pattern — generate WHERE clauses, JOINs, or column lists:

# macros/recent_orders_filter.sql
{% macro recent_orders_filter(date_column, days_back=30) %}
    {{ date_column }} >= current_date - interval '{{ days_back }} days'
{% endmacro %}

# Use in WHERE clause:
select * 
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
where {{ recent_orders_filter('order_date', days_back=90) }}

# Useful when filter logic is shared across many models

Macros calling other macros

# macros/usd_revenue.sql
{% macro usd_revenue(amount_cents_col, fx_rate_col=1) %}
    {{ cents_to_dollars(amount_cents_col) }} * {{ fx_rate_col }}
{% endmacro %}

# Uses the cents_to_dollars macro from earlier
select
    order_id,
    {{ usd_revenue('amount_cents', 'fx_rate_to_usd') }} as revenue_usd
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

The dbt_utils package — pre-built macros

Install dbt_utils to get dozens of useful macros built by the community:

# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.1.1

# Run dbt deps to install
# Then use anywhere:

# Generate a surrogate key from columns
{{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id', 'order_date']) }}

# Pivot a column dynamically (no hardcoded list)
{{ dbt_utils.pivot(
    column='status',
    values=dbt_utils.get_column_values(table=ref('stg_orders'), column='status')
) }}

# Union all tables matching a pattern
{{ dbt_utils.union_relations(
    relations=[ref('stg_us_orders'), ref('stg_eu_orders'), ref('stg_apac_orders')]
) }}

# Star (select all columns except some)
select 
    {{ dbt_utils.star(from=ref('stg_orders'), except=['internal_id', 'created_by']) }}
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# Date spine for dim_date
{{ dbt_utils.date_spine(
    datepart="day",
    start_date="cast('2020-01-01' as date)",
    end_date="cast('2030-12-31' as date)"
) }}

Custom generic tests as macros

Generic tests are just macros with a specific signature. Custom test example:

# macros/test_positive_value.sql
{% test positive_value(model, column_name) %}
    select *
    from {{ model }}
    where {{ column_name }} <= 0
{% endtest %}

# Use in schema.yml like a built-in test:
columns:
  - name: amount_usd
    tests:
      - positive_value
      - not_null

Hook macros — run code before/after models

# Set a session variable before each model runs
# In dbt_project.yml:
models:
  +pre-hook: "set session_label = 'dbt_run_{{ invocation_id }}'"
  +post-hook: 
    - "grant select on {{ this }} to role analyst"
    - "grant select on {{ this }} to role bi_tool"

# Or define complex hooks as macros:
# macros/grant_select.sql
{% macro grant_select(role) %}
    grant select on {{ this }} to role {{ role }}
{% endmacro %}

# In dbt_project.yml:
models:
  marts:
    +post-hook: "{{ grant_select('analyst') }}"

Where to put macros

Organize by purpose:

macros/
├── transformations/
│   ├── cents_to_dollars.sql
│   └── usd_revenue.sql
├── tests/
│   ├── positive_value.sql
│   └── valid_date_range.sql
├── audit/
│   └── grant_select.sql
└── utilities/
    └── current_dbt_user.sql

When NOT to write a macro

  • One-off SQL — if you'll only use it once, inline is clearer
  • Trivial wrappers — SUM(x) doesn't need a macro
  • Logic that's likely to diverge — premature DRY-ing causes pain later
  • When dbt_utils already has it — reach for the package first
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a macro with a default argument, and what it compiles to
{% macro safe_divide(numerator, denominator, default_value=0) %}
    case when {{ denominator }} = 0 then {{ default_value }} else {{ numerator }} / {{ denominator }} end
{% endmacro %}
$ cat macros/cents_to_dollars.sql; echo; echo '-- fct_orders line, compiled:'; grep -n -B2 'as amount_usd' target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/fct_orders.sql {% macro cents_to_dollars(column_name, decimals=2) %} round({{ column_name }} / 100.0, {{ decimals }}) {% endmacro %} -- fct_orders line, compiled: 9- 10- round(amount_cents / 100.0, 2) 11: as amount_usd,
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: cents_to_dollars takes a column name and an optional number of decimals; safe_divide wraps a division in a CASE so a zero denominator returns a default instead of an error. Called from a model, the macro is replaced by the SQL fragment it returns, which the compiled fct_orders shows in place. Every model that needs the conversion calls the macro, so the rule lives in one file.

▸ BUILDING A MACRO LIBRARY
# Typical first macros for a new dbt project:

# 1. Money/units
{% macro cents_to_dollars(col) %}{{ col }} / 100.0{% endmacro %}
{% macro seconds_to_hours(col) %}{{ col }} / 3600.0{% endmacro %}

# 2. Date convenience
{% macro fiscal_year(date_col) %}
    case 
        when extract(month from {{ date_col }}) >= 5 
        then extract(year from {{ date_col }})
        else extract(year from {{ date_col }}) - 1
    end
{% endmacro %}

# 3. Safe operations
{% macro safe_divide(num, denom) %}...{% endmacro %}
{% macro safe_cast_int(col) %}
    try_cast({{ col }} as int)
{% endmacro %}

# 4. Business logic shared across models
{% macro is_business_user(email_col) %}
    {{ email_col }} not like '%@gmail.com'
    and {{ email_col }} not like '%@yahoo.com'
    and {{ email_col }} not like '%@hotmail.com'
{% endmacro %}

# Used everywhere consistently — change definition once.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Macros = reusable Jinja/SQL functions in macros/ folder
  • Definition: {% macro name(args) %}body{% endmacro %}
  • Call: {{ name(arg1, arg2) }} from any model
  • Support default args, keyword args, calling other macros
  • dbt_utils package has dozens of pre-built macros (surrogate_key, pivot, star, date_spine)
  • Custom generic tests are macros with {% test %} signature
  • Hooks (pre/post) run macros before/after model materialization
  • Don't over-DRY — one-off SQL is clearer inline

Schema override: generate_schema_name is a macro HOOK dbt calls for every model — override it in your project to control exactly which schema each model lands in per environment.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Variables and environment-specific configuration let one dbt project behave differently in dev, staging, and prod. Master this and you can write code that's fast in dev (small samples) and complete in prod (full data) — without forking the project.

Three variable scopes

VARIABLE SCOPES
Project vars: vars: in dbt_project.yml
Runtime vars: --vars on CLI
Env vars: environment variables via env_var()

Project variables in dbt_project.yml

# dbt_project.yml
vars:
  start_date: '2020-01-01'
  exclude_test_users: true
  high_value_threshold: 1000
  email_domains_to_exclude:
    - 'gmail.com'
    - 'yahoo.com'

# In models, access via var():
select * 
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where order_date >= '{{ var("start_date") }}'

# var() can take a default if not set:
where amount >= {{ var('high_value_threshold', 500) }}

Per-package variables

# Nest variables under package names for isolation:
vars:
  my_dbt_project:
    start_date: '2020-01-01'
  dbt_date:
    'dbt_date:time_zone': 'America/New_York'

# Now my_dbt_project's start_date doesn't conflict with another package's

Runtime variables via --vars

# Override project vars at runtime
dbt run --vars '{start_date: 2025-01-01}'

# Multiple vars (YAML inline)
dbt run --vars '{start_date: 2025-01-01, exclude_test_users: false}'

# Useful for:
# - Backfilling: dbt run --vars 'start_date: 2020-01-01' --select fct_orders
# - Testing alternate configs without editing files
# - CI overriding values per environment

Environment variables with env_var()

# In profiles.yml — never hardcode secrets:
password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') }}"

# In models — for environment-specific URLs, account IDs, etc:
{% set s3_bucket = env_var('S3_BUCKET', 'default-bucket') %}
copy into stg_external from '{{ s3_bucket }}/orders/'

# Set in shell:
export SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD='secret123'
export S3_BUCKET='prod-data-lake'

# Or use a .env file (gitignored) with dotenv tooling

target.* — environment context

The target object is automatically available in all models. Contains info about the current run:

# target.name      → 'dev', 'prod', etc.
# target.schema    → the active schema
# target.database  → the active database
# target.user      → the user running dbt
# target.type      → 'snowflake', 'bigquery', etc.

# Common pattern — limit data in dev:
select *
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
{% if target.name == 'dev' %}
  -- only last 30 days in dev for speed
  where order_date >= current_date - 30
{% endif %}

# Different schemas per env:
{{ config(
    schema='analytics' if target.name == 'prod' else 'dev_' ~ target.user
) }}

The dev/prod pattern

Most teams use this pattern in dbt_project.yml + models:

# dbt_project.yml
vars:
  # Default: use full data
  date_filter_days: 9999

# Override in dev for speed
# CI or local dev can call: dbt run --vars 'date_filter_days: 30'

# In model:
select *
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where order_date >= current_date - {{ var('date_filter_days') }}

Conditional materialization by env

# Heavy model: table in prod, view in dev (faster iteration)
{{ config(
    materialized='table' if target.name == 'prod' else 'view'
) }}

# Heavy model: incremental in prod, full in dev (simpler debugging)
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental' if target.name == 'prod' else 'table',
    unique_key='order_id'
) }}

Custom schema names

By default, dbt writes to <target_schema>_<custom_schema>. Override via macro:

# macros/generate_schema_name.sql
{% macro generate_schema_name(custom_schema_name, node) -%}
    {%- set default_schema = target.schema -%}
    {%- if target.name == 'prod' and custom_schema_name is not none -%}
        {{ custom_schema_name | trim }}
    {%- else -%}
        {{ default_schema }}{%- if custom_schema_name is not none -%}_{{ custom_schema_name | trim }}{%- endif -%}
    {%- endif -%}
{%- endmacro %}

# Now in prod: schema is exactly the custom_schema (e.g., 'marts')
# In dev: schema is 'dev_natasha_marts' (your sandbox + custom)

Per-env credentials with separate profiles

# profiles.yml — multiple targets per profile
my_project:
  target: dev
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: snowflake
      role: ANALYTICS_DEV
      schema: dev_natasha
      threads: 4
    
    ci:
      type: snowflake
      role: ANALYTICS_CI
      schema: "dbt_cloud_pr_{{ env_var('PR_NUMBER', 'local') }}"
      threads: 8
    
    prod:
      type: snowflake
      role: ANALYTICS_PROD
      schema: analytics
      threads: 16
★ TARGET-AWARE DEFAULTS

Pattern: write code that "does the right thing" automatically based on target. Dev = fast, sample. Prod = complete, real. CI = isolated, ephemeral. The model author shouldn't need to remember dev hacks — bake them in.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same model compiled with a runtime var and with the prod target
$ dbt compile --select fct_orders --vars {start_date: 2026-03-01} Compiled node 'fct_orders' is: with __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined as ( select o.*, c.segment, c.country from "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__orders" o left join "warehouse"."dev_natasha"."stg_app__customers" c using (customer_id) ) select order_id, customer_id, product, round(amount_cents / 100.0, 2) as amount_usd, status, segment, ordered_at from __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined where ordered_at >= '2026-03-01' $ grep -n 'ordered_at >=' target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/fct_orders.sql 16:where ordered_at >= '2026-03-01' $ dbt compile --select fct_orders --target prod Compiled node 'fct_orders' is: with __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined as ( select o.*, c.segment, c.country from "warehouse"."analytics"."stg_app__orders" o left join "warehouse"."analytics"."stg_app__customers" c using (customer_id) ) select order_id, customer_id, product, round(amount_cents / 100.0, 2) as amount_usd, status, segment, ordered_at from __dbt__cte__int_orders__joined where ordered_at >= '2026-01-01' and status != 'test' $ grep -n -A3 'ordered_at >=' target/compiled/crteam/models/marts/fct_orders.sql 16:where ordered_at >= '2026-01-01' 17- 18- and status != 'test'
actual output, captured from dbt-core 1.12 with the dbt-duckdb adapter

Walk through it: --vars overrides the project's start_date for one command, and the compiled WHERE clause shows the new date. ◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Snapshots are dbt's native SCD2 implementation. They let you track how source data changes over time — without rolling your own version-tracking logic. Critical for analyzing historical state ("what was this customer's segment when they placed that order?") and for audit/compliance.

What snapshots do

Snapshots periodically check a source table for changes. When they find changes, they insert NEW rows with effective-date columns, preserving the old version. Result: a full history of every change.

SNAPSHOT BEHAVIOR
First run: copies all source rows into snapshot table, adds metadata columns
Subsequent runs: detects changes; closes old row's valid_to; inserts new row

Result: SCD Type 2 — full history with dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to columns

Basic snapshot syntax

# snapshots/customers_snapshot.sql

{% snapshot customers_snapshot %}

{{
    config(
      target_schema='snapshots',
      unique_key='customer_id',
      strategy='check',
      check_cols=['segment', 'email', 'country']
    )
}}

select * from {{ source('app', 'customers') }}

{% endsnapshot %}

Required config: strategy

Two strategies for detecting changes:

check Compare specified columns. Use when source has no reliable updated_at.
timestamp Use source's updated_at column. More efficient when available. 
# Check strategy
{{ config(
    target_schema='snapshots',
    unique_key='customer_id',
    strategy='check',
    check_cols=['segment', 'email', 'country']    # explicit list
) }}

# Or check ALL columns
check_cols='all'

# Timestamp strategy (more efficient)
{{ config(
    target_schema='snapshots',
    unique_key='customer_id',
    strategy='timestamp',
    updated_at='updated_at'    # source column to track
) }}

Running snapshots

# Run all snapshots
dbt snapshot

# Run specific snapshot
dbt snapshot --select customers_snapshot

# Snapshots are NOT run by dbt run — they're separate
# Schedule them on their own cadence (often more frequent than models)

What the snapshot table looks like

# After first run:
| customer_id | segment   | email           | country | dbt_valid_from | dbt_valid_to | dbt_scd_id |
| C42         | small_biz | alice@old.com   | US      | 2024-01-15     | NULL         | hash1      |
| C18         | small_biz | bob@email.com   | UK      | 2024-02-20     | NULL         | hash2      |

# After C42 upgrades to enterprise (run snapshot again):
| customer_id | segment    | email           | country | dbt_valid_from | dbt_valid_to | dbt_scd_id |
| C42         | small_biz  | alice@old.com   | US      | 2024-01-15     | 2025-04-15   | hash1      |
| C42         | enterprise | alice@old.com   | US      | 2025-04-15     | NULL         | hash3      |
| C18         | small_biz  | bob@email.com   | UK      | 2024-02-20     | NULL         | hash2      |

# Old row's dbt_valid_to is now set; new row added.
# Current rows: dbt_valid_to IS NULL

Querying snapshot history

# Current state — most common use:
select *
from {{ ref('customers_snapshot') }}
where dbt_valid_to is null

# As of a specific date:
select *
from {{ ref('customers_snapshot') }}
where '2025-03-01' between dbt_valid_from 
                        and coalesce(dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31')

# Full history of one customer:
select *
from {{ ref('customers_snapshot') }}
where customer_id = 'C42'
order by dbt_valid_from

Using snapshots in dim models

Don't expose raw snapshot tables to analysts. Build a clean dim on top:

# models/marts/dim_customers.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id', 'dbt_valid_from']) }} as customer_sk,
    customer_id,
    segment,
    email,
    country,
    dbt_valid_from as valid_from,
    coalesce(dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31') as valid_to,
    dbt_valid_to is null as is_current
from {{ ref('customers_snapshot') }}

Joining facts to SCD2 dims

# "As-was" — customer segment AT THE TIME of order
select
    o.order_id,
    c.segment as segment_at_order_time,
    o.amount
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} o
join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c
    on c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    and o.order_date between c.valid_from and c.valid_to

# "Current state" — customer's segment NOW
select
    o.order_id,
    c.segment as current_segment,
    o.amount
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} o
join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c
    on c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    and c.is_current = true

Scheduling snapshots

Snapshots should run BEFORE the models that depend on them. Typical schedule:

# Daily snapshot job (3am):
dbt snapshot

# Daily build job (4am):
dbt build

# Or combined in one job:
dbt snapshot
dbt build

# In dbt Cloud / Airflow: snapshots = separate task, runs before build

Common snapshot pitfalls

⚠ WATCH OUT FOR
  • Snapshot only runs when you tell it to. A model can't trigger a snapshot. Always schedule snapshots separately.
  • Hard deletes are NOT captured. If a row disappears from source, snapshot still shows it as current. Use invalidate_hard_deletes: true config.
  • Changing check_cols list breaks history. Adding/removing tracked columns can create false changes.
  • Snapshots live in their OWN schema — usually snapshots. They're not models.
  • Big sources = expensive snapshots. Time-series tables (billion rows) should NOT be snapshotted directly. Snapshot a filtered/summarized version.

Hard delete handling

# If source rows can be deleted (not just updated), enable:
{{ config(
    target_schema='snapshots',
    unique_key='customer_id',
    strategy='check',
    check_cols=['segment', 'email'],
    invalidate_hard_deletes=true
) }}

# Now if a row vanishes from source, dbt sets its dbt_valid_to
# (treating disappearance as a "change")

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

dbt builds the models, but something needs to TRIGGER dbt — on a schedule, after upstream pipelines, or on commits to main. Choosing the right orchestrator shapes your operational maturity. There's no one right answer; the trade-offs are real.

The orchestration options

dbt Cloud Hosted by dbt Labs. Scheduling, CI, docs, IDE. Easiest. Paid.
Airflow Industry standard. Python DAG definitions. Powerful but complex.
Prefect Python-native, simpler than Airflow. Hybrid cloud/self-hosted.
Dagster Asset-based. Excellent dbt integration. Modern alternative.
GitHub Actions Free for public repos. Good for scheduled runs + CI. Limited at scale.
cron Simple Linux schedule. Fine for solo projects. No retry/observability.

dbt Cloud — the easiest path

# Setup:
# 1. Connect your GitHub repo
# 2. Configure profiles in dbt Cloud UI (not profiles.yml locally)
# 3. Create environments: dev, ci, prod
# 4. Create jobs:
#    - "daily build": dbt build, cron 0 4 * * *
#    - "hourly snapshot": dbt snapshot, cron 0 * * * *
#    - "CI": dbt build --select state:modified+ on every PR
# 5. Connect Slack/email for alerts

# Cost: $100-1500/mo depending on seats + features
# Pros: zero infra, scheduling+CI+docs+IDE in one
# Cons: vendor lock-in, runs limited by tier

Airflow + dbt

# Airflow DAG example
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime

with DAG(
    'dbt_daily',
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    schedule_interval='0 4 * * *',
    catchup=False
) as dag:
    
    dbt_seed = BashOperator(
        task_id='dbt_seed',
        bash_command='cd /opt/dbt && dbt seed --target prod'
    )
    
    dbt_snapshot = BashOperator(
        task_id='dbt_snapshot',
        bash_command='cd /opt/dbt && dbt snapshot --target prod'
    )
    
    dbt_run = BashOperator(
        task_id='dbt_run',
        bash_command='cd /opt/dbt && dbt run --target prod'
    )
    
    dbt_test = BashOperator(
        task_id='dbt_test',
        bash_command='cd /opt/dbt && dbt test --target prod'
    )
    
    dbt_seed >> dbt_snapshot >> dbt_run >> dbt_test

# Better: use the dbt-cosmos or airflow-dbt provider for finer-grained tasks
# (one Airflow task per dbt model)

GitHub Actions — free + simple

# .github/workflows/dbt_daily.yml
name: dbt daily build
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 4 * * *'   # 4am UTC
  workflow_dispatch:       # manual trigger

jobs:
  dbt_build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - name: dbt deps
        run: dbt deps
      - name: dbt build
        env:
          SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
        run: dbt build --target prod

Choosing the right orchestrator

DECISION FRAMEWORK
Solo / small team, no infra appetite: dbt Cloud
Small team, want free: GitHub Actions
Data team owns infrastructure: Airflow or Dagster
Many other pipelines + want one orchestrator: Airflow
Heavy dbt + asset-oriented: Dagster
Need quickly + Python-native: Prefect

Environments

Every orchestrator setup needs at least three environments:

dev Developers' sandbox schemas. Manual runs. Per-user.
ci PR validation. Ephemeral per-PR schemas. Auto-deletes.
prod Scheduled runs. Real consumers. Tight access control.

dbt build vs separate commands

# dbt build runs in DAG order, fails fast:
# - seeds → snapshots → models → tests
# - If a test fails on stg_orders, dependent fct_orders won't run

dbt build --target prod

# vs separate commands (legacy pattern):
dbt seed --target prod
dbt snapshot --target prod
dbt run --target prod
dbt test --target prod
# Tests run AFTER all models — failures don't stop downstream

# Modern recommendation: use dbt build

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

CI/CD for dbt catches mistakes before they hit production. Every PR runs your tests on the proposed changes; broken changes can't merge. This is the difference between "we hope it works" and "we know it works." Critical for teams of 3+ to function without constant breakage.

What CI does for dbt

When you open a PR, CI automatically:

  1. Builds your modified models against a CI environment
  2. Runs all tests on the built models
  3. Reports results back to the PR (✓ or ✗)
  4. Blocks merge if anything fails
CI WORKFLOW
PR opened → dbt builds ONLY modified models in isolated schema → all tests run
→ Results posted to PR → if pass, allowed to merge → on merge, prod runs full DAG

Slim CI — only build what changed

Building the whole DAG on every PR is slow and expensive. Slim CI uses --select state:modified+ to build only changed models and their dependencies:

# Slim CI command
dbt build \
  --select state:modified+ \
  --defer \
  --state ./prod_manifest \
  --target ci

# What this does:
# --select state:modified+
#     Build only models that changed in this PR, plus downstream dependents
# --defer
#     For unchanged upstream models, reference PROD versions (don't rebuild)
# --state ./prod_manifest
#     Where to find the prod manifest.json for comparison

# Result: 3-minute CI instead of 30-minute full DAG

Getting the prod manifest

Slim CI needs a baseline manifest.json from a recent prod run. Typically:

# In production job: after every run, upload manifest.json to S3/GCS
aws s3 cp target/manifest.json s3://my-artifacts/dbt/prod/manifest.json

# In CI: download before running dbt
aws s3 cp s3://my-artifacts/dbt/prod/manifest.json ./prod_manifest/manifest.json
dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod_manifest --target ci

GitHub Actions CI workflow

# .github/workflows/dbt_ci.yml
name: dbt CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - '**.sql'
      - '**.yml'
      - 'dbt_project.yml'
      - 'packages.yml'

jobs:
  dbt_test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.11' }
      
      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      
      - name: Configure AWS (for manifest)
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_CI_ROLE }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      
      - name: Download prod manifest
        run: |
          mkdir prod_manifest
          aws s3 cp s3://my-artifacts/dbt/prod/manifest.json prod_manifest/
      
      - name: dbt deps
        run: dbt deps
      
      - name: dbt build (Slim CI)
        env:
          SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: |
          dbt build \
            --select state:modified+ \
            --defer \
            --state ./prod_manifest \
            --target ci

Per-PR sandboxes

Each PR's CI run uses its own schema so concurrent PRs don't conflict:

# profiles.yml
ci:
  type: snowflake
  role: ANALYTICS_CI
  schema: "dbt_cloud_pr_{{ env_var('PR_NUMBER', 'manual') }}"
  threads: 8

# Schema becomes: dbt_cloud_pr_123, dbt_cloud_pr_124, etc.

# Cleanup: schedule a job to drop old CI schemas (e.g., older than 14 days)

CD — deployment on merge

# On merge to main, trigger production deployment

# .github/workflows/dbt_deploy.yml
name: dbt deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.11' }
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      
      # Option A: trigger dbt Cloud job via API
      - name: Trigger dbt Cloud deploy
        run: |
          curl -X POST "https://cloud.getdbt.com/api/v2/accounts/${ACCOUNT}/jobs/${JOB_ID}/run/" \
            -H "Authorization: Token ${{ secrets.DBT_CLOUD_TOKEN }}"
      
      # Option B: run dbt directly
      - name: dbt build prod
        env:
          SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PROD_PASSWORD }}
        run: dbt build --target prod

      # After successful run: upload new manifest for future CI
      - run: aws s3 cp target/manifest.json s3://my-artifacts/dbt/prod/

What to check in CI beyond dbt build

Production-grade CI also includes:

  • SQLFluff lint — enforces SQL style (lowercase keywords, indent rules)
  • dbt-project-evaluator — checks for anti-patterns (no description, missing tests)
  • YAML lint — schema.yml well-formed
  • Pre-commit hooks — catch issues locally before pushing
# SQLFluff in CI
- name: Lint SQL
  run: |
    pip install sqlfluff
    sqlfluff lint models/

# dbt-project-evaluator
# Add to packages.yml:
# - package: dbt-labs/dbt_project_evaluator
#   version: 0.10.0

# Run as a model:
dbt run --select package:dbt_project_evaluator
dbt test --select package:dbt_project_evaluator

  - repo: https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff
    rev: 3.0.0
    hooks:

Pair CI with GitHub branch protection so failing checks block merge:

★ FAST CI = HAPPY DEVELOPERS

If CI takes 30 minutes, people stop running it locally and just push to see if it passes. Aim for <5 minute CI. Slim CI is the main lever. Parallelism and caching help too.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Once dbt runs in production, something will break. Your job: notice it fast, find the cause faster, fix it. Good logging, alerting, and performance tracking turn a noisy debugging fire-drill into a 5-minute investigation.

dbt's built-in logging

Every dbt run produces logs at multiple levels:

# Console output: human-readable summary
dbt run
# 14:23:01  Running with dbt=1.7.0
# 14:23:02  Found 47 models, 95 tests
# 14:23:03  Concurrency: 8 threads
# 14:23:03  1 of 47 START sql view model staging.stg_orders [RUN]
# 14:23:04  1 of 47 OK created sql view model staging.stg_orders [0.42s]
# ...
# 14:25:14  Completed successfully

# Detailed logs: logs/dbt.log (with verbose detail)
# Full SQL of every operation, timing, errors

# Structured artifacts in target/:
#   run_results.json  ← outcome of last run
#   manifest.json     ← project metadata + lineage
#   catalog.json      ← column-level info (after dbt docs generate)
#   sources.json      ← source freshness results

run_results.json

The most useful artifact for monitoring. Contains a JSON record of every node that ran:

# target/run_results.json (excerpt)
{
  "results": [
    {
      "unique_id": "model.my_project.fct_orders",
      "status": "success",
      "execution_time": 12.4,
      "thread_id": "Thread-1",
      "timing": [
        {"name": "compile", "started_at": "...", "completed_at": "..."},
        {"name": "execute", "started_at": "...", "completed_at": "..."}
      ],
      "adapter_response": {
        "rows_affected": 1234567,
        "bytes_processed": 1024000000
      }
    },
    ...
  ]
}

# Parse this to track:
# - Which models slowest? (execution_time)
# - Row counts changing dramatically? (rows_affected)
# - Cost trends? (bytes_processed)

Setting up alerts

dbt Cloud Built-in Slack + email + webhook notifications on job success/failure/warning
Airflow Configure on_failure_callback per task or DAG-wide
GitHub Actions Use slackapi/slack-github-action on failure step
Custom Parse run_results.json, post to PagerDuty/Slack/Opsgenie

Slack alert from GitHub Actions

# In dbt_daily.yml
- name: dbt build
  run: dbt build --target prod
  id: dbt_build

- name: Notify Slack on failure
  if: failure()
  uses: slackapi/slack-github-action@v1
  with:
    channel-id: 'C01234567'
    slack-message: |
      🚨 dbt prod run failed
      Job: ${{ github.workflow }}
      Run: ${{ github.run_id }}
      View: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
  env:
    SLACK_BOT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN }}

What to alert on

ALERT SEVERITY
P0 (page someone): prod dbt run failed entirely
P1 (Slack channel): test failures in prod; source freshness errors
P2 (daily digest): slow models trending slower; warning-level tests
P3 (weekly review): cost trends; long-running models; flaky tests

Source freshness

Detect when sources haven't been updated — usually the upstream pipeline broke:

# models/staging/_sources.yml
sources:
  - name: app
    tables:
      - name: orders
        loaded_at_field: created_at
        freshness:
          warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}

# Check freshness
dbt source freshness
# Reports pass/warn/error per source
# Schedule this hourly; alert on errors

Tracking model performance over time

Build a "dbt run history" table by parsing run_results.json after each run:

# After each prod run, ingest run_results into a tracking table:
# A simple Python script:

import json
import snowflake.connector
from datetime import datetime

with open('target/run_results.json') as f:
    results = json.load(f)

conn = snowflake.connector.connect(...)
cur = conn.cursor()

for r in results['results']:
    cur.execute("""
        INSERT INTO meta.dbt_run_history (
            run_id, node_id, status, execution_time, 
            rows_affected, run_started_at
        ) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
    """, (
        results['args']['invocation_id'],
        r['unique_id'],
        r['status'],
        r['execution_time'],
        r['adapter_response'].get('rows_affected'),
        datetime.now()
    ))

# Now you can query:
# SELECT node_id, AVG(execution_time) as avg_time, MAX(execution_time)
# FROM meta.dbt_run_history
# WHERE run_started_at >= current_date - 30
# GROUP BY node_id
# ORDER BY avg_time DESC LIMIT 10;
# → top 10 slowest models trending

Elementary — pre-built observability

If you don't want to build your own, install Elementary:

# packages.yml
- package: elementary-data/elementary
  version: 0.15.0

# Adds:
# - dbt run history tracking
# - Anomaly detection on row counts, column nulls, etc.
# - Slack/Teams alerts on test failures
# - Browser-based dashboard
# - Snapshots of source freshness

# Free tier covers most teams.

Debugging a failed model

The investigation flow:

  1. Read the error message in console / dbt.log
  2. Check target/compiled/ — see the actual SQL that was sent
  3. Run the compiled SQL directly in your warehouse UI
  4. Inspect parent models — did upstream data change?
  5. Compare to recent successful runs via run history
# Quick debug commands:

# What's the exact SQL?
dbt compile --select my_failing_model
cat target/compiled/my_project/models/my_failing_model.sql

# What did the run say?
cat logs/dbt.log | grep my_failing_model

# Try it in isolation:
dbt run --select my_failing_model --full-refresh

# Did parents succeed?
dbt run --select +my_failing_model

Walk through it: every dbt command writes target/run_results.json: one entry per node with its status and how long it took. A monitor reads this file, not the console: a status other than success or pass triggers the alert, and the execution times, stored run after run, are how you notice a model that used to take twelve seconds now taking twelve minutes.

★ ALWAYS START WITH target/compiled/

Most "weird" dbt failures become obvious when you read the compiled SQL. Jinja did something unexpected, a ref resolved wrong, a macro produced bad output — it's all visible in target/compiled/<project>/<path>.sql.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • dbt produces logs/dbt.log + structured artifacts in target/
  • run_results.json = key file for monitoring (status, timing, row counts)
  • Alert tiers: P0 (page), P1 (Slack), P2 (daily), P3 (weekly review)
  • dbt source freshness detects upstream pipeline failures
  • Build a dbt_run_history table by parsing run_results.json
  • Elementary package provides observability out of the box
  • Debug flow: error msg → target/compiled/ → run in warehouse UI → check parents
  • 90% of dbt debugging happens in target/compiled/

TermDefinition
staging/1:1 with sources, light cleaning, prefixed stg_
intermediate/joins, transformations, business logic, prefixed int_

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Knowing dbt syntax isn't enough — you need to know how to USE it well. Real dbt projects follow patterns that scale: layered architecture, clear naming, materialization choices, modular code. The anti-patterns silently kill productivity. This is the wisdom that separates juniors from staff engineers.

The staging → intermediate → marts pattern

Every dbt project should follow this layered convention:

THE LAYERS
staging/ — 1:1 with sources, light cleaning, prefixed stg_
intermediate/ — joins, transformations, business logic, prefixed int_
marts/ — final user-facing models, prefixed fct_ or dim_ 
# Materialization defaults per layer (dbt_project.yml):
models:
  my_project:
    staging:
      +materialized: view          # cheap, always fresh
      +schema: staging
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral     # compiled into downstream queries
    marts:
      +materialized: table         # fast queries for end users
      +schema: marts

Naming conventions that scale

Pattern Examples
stg_<source>__<entity> stg_stripe__charges, stg_app__orders
int_<area>_<purpose> int_orders_with_refunds, int_users_enriched
fct_<event> fct_orders, fct_page_views
dim_<entity> dim_customers, dim_products
Columns: snake_case, units in name amount_usd, duration_sec, is_active

Materialization decision flow

# Decision tree:

# 1. Is this an intermediate building block used by other models only?
#    YES → ephemeral

# 2. Is the data <10M rows AND queried infrequently?
#    YES → view (cheap, always fresh)

# 3. Is the data >10M rows OR queried often?
#    YES → table (worth materializing)

# 4. Is the table append-only AND >100M rows AND full refresh is slow?
#    YES → incremental

# 5. Special cases:
#    Need history? → snapshot
#    Materialized view product? (Snowflake dynamic table, BQ materialized view)
#      → use that adapter feature

Anti-pattern: the "one big model"

# ✗ BAD — 800 lines in a single model
# models/marts/fct_everything.sql
with raw_orders as (
    select * from raw.orders where status != 'test'    -- staging logic
),
with_customers as (
    select o.*, c.segment, c.country, ...               -- intermediate logic
    from raw_orders o join raw.customers c ...
),
with_products as (
    select wc.*, p.category, ...
    from with_customers wc join raw.products p ...
),
with_promotions as (
    -- ...100 more lines
),
final as (
    -- ...
)
select * from final

# ✓ GOOD — split into layers
# stg_app__orders.sql        ← cleaning
# stg_app__customers.sql     ← cleaning
# int_orders_with_context.sql ← joins
# fct_orders.sql             ← final mart, references int_

Anti-pattern: hardcoded names

# ✗ BAD
select * from analytics.stg_orders

# ✓ GOOD
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

# Always. There's no exception.

Anti-pattern: business logic in staging

# ✗ BAD — staging should be 1:1 with source
# models/staging/stg_orders.sql
select
    id as order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount / 100 as amount_usd,
    case when amount > 1000 then 'high' else 'normal' end as size_tier,  -- ❌ logic
    case when status in ('paid', 'shipped') then true else false end as is_revenue  -- ❌ logic
from raw.orders
where status != 'cancelled'  -- ❌ business filter

# ✓ GOOD — staging is dumb; logic in intermediate or marts
# stg_orders.sql:
select
    id as order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount_cents,
    status,
    created_at
from raw.orders

# int_orders_categorized.sql:
select
    *,
    amount_cents / 100.0 as amount_usd,
    case when amount_cents > 100000 then 'high' else 'normal' end as size_tier
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where status != 'cancelled'

Anti-pattern: skipping tests

# Minimum tests for every fact/dim:
- name: fct_orders
  columns:
    - name: order_id
      tests: [unique, not_null]
    - name: customer_id
      tests:
        - not_null
        - relationships:
            to: ref('dim_customers')
            field: customer_id

# Block PRs without tests via dbt-project-evaluator.
# It's not pedantic; it's how you sleep at night.

Anti-pattern: surrogate-key chaos

# ✗ BAD — inconsistent surrogate key generation
# stg_orders generates customer_sk one way:
select md5(customer_id) as customer_sk, ...

# dim_customers generates it another way:
select hash(customer_id::text) as customer_sk, ...

# Result: joins silently produce zero rows because the hashes don't match.

# ✓ GOOD — always use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key:
{{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id']) }} as customer_sk
# Same logic everywhere. Same hash. Joins work.

Refactoring inherited models

You'll inherit messy dbt projects. The refactor playbook:

  1. Write tests that pass on current state — your safety net
  2. Build new versions alongside — fct_orders_v2.sql
  3. Compare row-by-row — use dbt audit_helper to confirm parity
  4. Migrate consumers one at a time — update each Tableau workbook
  5. Deprecate the old version — once nothing references it
  6. Repeat — never rewrite "everything at once"

The audit_helper package

# packages.yml
- package: dbt-labs/audit_helper
  version: 0.11.0

# Compare two models row-by-row:
# analyses/compare_orders.sql
{{ audit_helper.compare_relations(
    a_relation=ref('fct_orders'),
    b_relation=ref('fct_orders_v2'),
    primary_key='order_id'
) }}

# Returns categorized differences:
# - identical
# - in_a_only
# - in_b_only  
# - different_values

# Run before migrating consumers

The dbt project evolution timeline

# Months 0-3: Bootstrap
# - 1-5 sources, 10-30 models
# - Single layer (just marts)
# - Manual runs, no CI

# Months 3-9: Foundation
# - Add staging/intermediate/marts split
# - Add basic tests (unique, not_null on PKs)
# - Set up CI
# - Add docs
# - Schedule daily prod run

# Months 9-18: Maturity
# - 100+ models
# - Per-PR CI sandboxes
# - Snapshots for SCD2 dims
# - Slim CI with --defer
# - dbt-project-evaluator enforced
# - Slack alerting

# 18+: Scale
# - 500+ models, multiple repos / domains
# - Cross-team conventions doc
# - Semantic layer or metric framework
# - Data lineage to BI tools
# - SLOs on key marts
★ CONSISTENCY OVER PERFECTION

A pragmatic, consistent dbt project beats a perfect one no one follows. Pick conventions early, write them down in a CONVENTIONS.md, and enforce them in CI. Iterate as the team learns.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the layers as dbt sees them
models:
  crteam:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral
    marts:
      +materialized: table
$ dbt ls --resource-type model --output json --output-keys name config 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys, json; [print(d['name'].ljust(24), d['config']['materialized']) for d in map(json.loads, (l for l in sys.stdin if l.startswith('{')))]" dim_customers table fct_events incremental fct_orders table int_orders__joined ephemeral rpt_product_pivot table stg_app__customers view stg_app__events view stg_app__orders view

Walk through it: the folder a model sits in decides its default: staging models are cheap views that rename and type, intermediate models are ephemeral building blocks, marts are tables the dashboards read. dbt ls confirms the materialization each model ended up with, and the naming does the rest: stg_ for staging, int_ for intermediate, fct_ and dim_ for marts, rpt_ for reports.

▸ A WELL-RUN DBT PROJECT
# Observable signs:
# ✓ models/ has staging/intermediate/marts structure
# ✓ Every model has unique+not_null on its grain key
# ✓ Every mart has a description with grain declared
# ✓ packages.yml uses dbt_utils + dbt-project-evaluator
# ✓ Branch protection blocks PRs without CI green
# ✓ Slim CI runs in <5 minutes
# ✓ Prod runs are scheduled + alert on failure
# ✓ Source freshness is monitored
# ✓ Docs site is published + linked in README
# ✓ CONVENTIONS.md exists and is followed
# ✓ No model file > 200 lines
# ✓ Surrogate keys consistently use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key
# ✓ profiles.yml is gitignored or uses env_var() throughout

# If any are missing, that's the next thing to fix.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Layer the project: staging (view) → intermediate (ephemeral) → marts (table)
  • Name consistently: stg_, int_, fct_, dim_
  • Materialize by use: ephemeral, view, table, incremental — by data size and query pattern
  • Avoid: one big model, hardcoded names, logic in staging, skipped tests
  • Use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key everywhere for consistency
  • Refactor inherited models with audit_helper to verify parity
  • Enforce conventions via dbt-project-evaluator in CI
  • Consistency over perfection — write CONVENTIONS.md, enforce in CI

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 dbt Foundations

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

What dbt Is and Why It Exists

What dbt is — dbt (data build tool) is the T in ELT — the transformation layer that runs inside your data warehouse. You write SQL files; dbt compiles them, runs them in dependency…

The ELT vs ETL shift — The fundamental shift dbt rides on:

The modern data stack — Sources (Postgres, Salesforce, Stripe, GA4, ...) ↓ Extract + Load tool (Fivetran, Airbyte, Meltano) ↓ Cloud warehouse (Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks / Redshift) ↓…
